The Four Teachings of Liao-Fan (Original Text)
The Four Teachings of Liao-Fan (Vernacular)
Note: The subheadings within the text were added by the translator.

Since ancient times, countless people have been bound by their fate and fortune, unable to act as their own masters. Only the greatly good cannot be bound by fate; this is why the sages possess the secret of creating their own destiny. The Four Teachings of Liao-Fan is known throughout the world as the precious canon of transforming one's destiny. Those of great blessings, by their inborn love of virtue, upon obtaining this book, are able to read it sincerely, never tiring of it, and to move from understanding to practice. Thus sickness turns to health, poverty to success, sin to blessing, and the ordinary to the sage. Using it to perfect oneself, anyone may become a sage; using it to perfect the world, the whole world may dispel its misfortunes. This is the most effective and practical path of self-liberation and liberating others.

The way of establishing oneself and the way of establishing the world lie herein; the way of transcending birth and death also lies herein. Those in the world with discerning eyes will never pass it by lightly. The learned, the ambitious, the accomplished, those with the great vow to clarify the universe and benefit all beings, upon seeing this book, cannot but rejoice and praise it, urging others to read and practice it. In this the genuine value of the book may be glimpsed.

The youth of today, do they not entertain grand ambitions and grand words, with the broad spirit of clarifying the universe, and yet end in achieving nothing, because the foundation is not established? The Four Teachings of Liao-Fan is truly the great foundation of establishing oneself, upholding one's calling, and governing the world! This book preaches by living example, teaching through real results. If one reads it thoroughly and practices it with effort, then destiny is established by oneself, blessing is created by oneself, and nothing in the world is hard. The worthy and the gentleman, obtaining this chapter, hold it fast in their hearts, and thereby turn their minds and open a path to the clouds from the very ground.

Know that punishing evil requires great power, but encouraging good anyone can do. Since the heart desires to do good, every direction leads to the Way; practicing deeply, one meets abundance everywhere. If one can truly be strict with oneself as an example and earnestly proclaim it, without spending a cent, the merit is greatest of all.

Moreover, blessing the people and turning back the calamities of this last age are the original virtue of our participation in the creative transformation of heaven and earth, the great root of ordering the family and governing the state. How can we toil for fame and profit and waste ourselves in self-abandonment? Besides, if you persuade one person to become a sage or a bodhisattva, then for the rest of that person's life, the good deeds accomplished cannot be counted, and the ignorant taught cannot be counted either. All this comes from the gentleman who awakened him, so his merit is equal to theirs. Compared with those who chase fame and profit and may never attain it, this is as far as heaven from earth!

Therefore it is said that the gift of the Dharma is greatest, and the power of the vow is endless. All who wish to plant a field of blessing, right before your eyes and beneath your feet is the opportunity. Human life is hard to obtain; the present condition is easily lost. I pray that all who see or hear this will together arouse a deep mind, press forward with effort, diligently cultivate, and preach it to others. Do not let this great opportunity pass by before your eyes and beneath your feet!

Yet to become a sage is not hard; it lies in illuminating one's own luminous virtue, which must begin with investigating things and extending knowledge. If the desires of the person cannot be vigorously eradicated, the innate true knowledge can never be fully manifested. To cause it to appear, one should in daily conduct and speech always maintain awareness, not allowing any contrary emotion or thought to arise in the mind even for a moment. Constantly keep the mind empty, serene, and clear, like a mirror on its stand, reflecting what comes before it without being turned by it. Beauty and ugliness belong to themselves; what concern are they to me? When it comes, do not anticipate; when it goes, do not cling. If contrary thoughts begin to stir, at once attack them sternly and eradicate them completely. As when facing an enemy army, not only do you not let them invade your territory, you must behead their generals, seize their banners, and destroy their remnant forces.

The method of commanding this army must begin with strict self-government. Do not be lax or negligent; restrain oneself and return to propriety, holding to reverence and sincerity. For weapons use the four don'ts of Yan Hui, the three daily reflections of Zengzi, and the few faults and awareness of error of Qu Boyu, adding the trembling caution of one facing a deep abyss or treading on thin ice, and so oppose the enemy army of contrary thoughts. Then the might of the army spreads far, and the enemy party is chilled with fear, dreading the extreme punishment of extermination and hoping for the great grace of amnesty. Thereupon they surrender one after another, fully repent their former minds, and cultivate their virtue. The general need not leave his tent, the soldiers need not bloody their blades; all enemies become children, and all rebels become good people. Following from above and imitated below, the whole land becomes peaceful, and without wielding weapons, one sits in great peace.

Master Yuan Liaofan's four teachings to his son are flowing in both matter and style, opening the mind to see clearly; reading them one feels a rising vigor and an eagerness to take them up, truly a fine counsel for the world. His words, 'Commit no evil, practice all good; establish your own destiny, seek your own blessing,' prevent the creator from monopolizing its power.

Having received and upheld the ledger of merit and demerit, he recorded every movement of thought, every word and deed, whether good or evil, in full detail, so as to increase good day by day and decrease evil. At first good and evil were mixed; over time only good remained and no evil. Thus he could turn no blessing into blessing, short life into long life, and no descendants into many descendants. In this life he entered the realm of the sages, and at death ascended to the Land of Ultimate Bliss; his conduct became a model for the world, his words a standard for the world. He was a great man, and so am I; how can I belittle myself and shrink back?

Since ancient times, countless people have been bound by fate and fortune, unable to act as their own masters. Only the greatly good cannot be bound by fate; this is why the sages possess the secret of transforming their destiny! The Four Teachings of Liao-Fan is known to all the world as the precious canon of transforming destiny. Those of great blessings, having an inborn love of virtue, upon obtaining this book, can read it sincerely, never tiring of it, and move from understanding to practice. Thus sickness turns to health, poverty to success, sin to blessing, and the ordinary to the sage. Using it to perfect oneself, one may fully become a sage; using it to perfect society, the whole society may dispel its misfortunes. This is the most practical and effective path of self-liberation and liberating others!

The way of accomplishing oneself and accomplishing society lies herein; the way of transcending the round of birth and death and escaping the three realms also lies herein. Those in the world with the eye of wisdom will never pass it by lightly. The learned, the ambitious, the accomplished, those with the great vow to clarify the universe and benefit all beings, upon seeing this book, cannot but rejoice and praise it, urging everyone they meet to read it and encouraging them to practice it. The precious value of this book may be glimpsed in this!

The youth of today, do they not entertain grand ambitions and grand words, with the broad spirit of clarifying the universe, yet in the end they achieve nothing, because their foundation is not established. The Four Teachings of Liao-Fan is truly the great foundation of establishing oneself, upholding one's calling, and governing the world! This book preaches by living example, teaching through real results. If one reads it thoroughly and practices it with effort, then destiny is created by oneself, blessing is made by oneself, and there is nothing in the world that cannot be done. The worthy and the gentleman, obtaining this chapter, treasure it in their hearts, and thereby turn their minds to open a path to the clouds from the very ground.

Know that punishing evil must be done by one of great power, but encouraging good anyone can do. Since the heart desires to do good, every direction leads to the Way; practicing to the depths, one meets abundance everywhere. If one can truly be strict with oneself as an example and earnestly proclaim it, without spending a cent of wealth, the merit is greatest of all.

Moreover, blessing the people and turning back the calamities of this last age are the original virtue of our participation in the creative transformation of heaven and earth, the great root of ordering the family and governing the state. How can we scheme for fame and profit rather than working greatly at cultivating virtue and urging goodness? This is destroying ourselves! Besides, if you persuade one person who later becomes a sage or bodhisattva, then for the rest of that life, the good deeds accomplished cannot be counted, and the ignorant people he teaches cannot be counted either. All this comes from the gentleman who awakened him, so your merit is equal to his. If you are strict with yourself as an example and earnestly proclaim it, compared with those who chase fame and profit and can never attain it, this is truly as far as heaven from earth!

Therefore it is said that the merit of preaching the true Dharma for others is greatest, and the power of the vow is endless. All who wish to cultivate merit and virtue, right before your eyes and beneath your feet is the opportunity. Human life is hard to obtain; the present condition is easily lost. I pray that all who see or hear this will together arouse a deep mind, press forward with effort, cultivate diligently, and proclaim it to others. Do not let this great opportunity slip past before your eyes and beneath your feet!

Yet to become a sage is not hard; it lies only in illuminating one's own bright and upright virtuous nature, which must begin with removing the desires of things and revealing the innate true knowledge of one's own mind. If the desires of things cannot be vigorously eradicated, the innate true knowledge can never be fully manifested. To cause it to appear, one should in daily affairs, in the arising of thought and all speech and action, always maintain awareness, not allowing any emotion or thought contrary to principle to arise in the mind even for a moment. Constantly keep the mind empty, serene, and clear, like a bright mirror on its stand, reflecting whatever is before it, without being turned by the external realm. Beauty and ugliness are their own affair; what has it to do with me? When it comes, there is no expectation; when it goes, there is no clinging and grief. If contrary thoughts have just begun to appear, at once attack them sternly and eradicate them completely, roots and all. As when facing an enemy army, not only do you not let them invade my land, you must behead their generals and seize their banners, and destroy their remnant forces.

The method of training and commanding this army must begin with strict self-government. One must not be slack or negligent; restrain one's seeing, hearing, speech, and action to accord with propriety, reverent and sincere. For weapons use the four don'ts of Yan Hui, the three daily reflections of Zengzi, and the few faults and awareness of error of Qu Boyu, adding the trembling caution of one facing a deep abyss or treading on thin ice, extremely careful and strict, opposing the enemy army of contrary thoughts. Then the might of the army spreads far, and the enemy party is chilled with fear, dreading the extreme calamity of the extermination of their kind and hoping for the great grace of pardon and amnesty. Thereupon they surrender one after another, turn their hearts, wash their minds, and become new people. Thus the general need not leave his tent, the soldiers need not bleed in battle; all enemies and rebels become good people. Following from above and imitated below, all turn from evil to the right; the four seas become clear and serene, and without war, the world is at peace.

Master Yuan Liaofan's four teachings to his son are flowing in both style and substance, awakening the mind and heart, making one feel a rising vigor and a craving to put them into practice, truly a precious canon for saving the world. The principle within, 'Commit no evil, practice all good, establish your own destiny, seek your own blessing,' can make us masters of our own destiny.

Master Liaofan received and upheld the ledger of merit and demerit; whenever a thought arose or a word or deed occurred, whether good or evil, he recorded it without the slightest omission, so as to ensure that good thoughts, words, and deeds increased daily, and evil thoughts, words, and deeds decreased daily. At first good and evil were still mixed; after long practice only good remained and no evil. Thus he could turn no blessing into blessing, early death into long life, and no descendants into many descendants. In life he was a worthy and a sage, and at death he was reborn in the highest grade in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; his conduct was a model for the masses, his words a standard for the world. Since Master Liaofan could thus transform his destiny and become a great man, so can I! How can I think lightly of myself, feel inferior, and shrink back?

blocks.text: The First Teaching: The Study of Establishing Destiny

inline.s: In my childhood I lost my father, and my mother commanded me to give up the pursuit of the examinations and study medicine, saying: 'It can nourish life and it can aid others; moreover, to master one art and gain a name by it was your father's lifelong wish.'

Later, at Ciyun Temple, I met an old man with a long beard and a majestic bearing, floating as an immortal; I paid him respect. He said to me: 'You are one destined for the official path. Next year you will enter the academy. Why do you not study?' I told him the reason and asked his name and dwelling. He said: 'My surname is Kong, and I am from Yunnan. I have received the authentic transmission of Shao Yong's Imperial Ultimate number, and it is my fate to transmit it to you.' I brought him home and told my mother, who said: 'Treat him well.'

I tested his numbers, and they were all verified to the smallest detail. So I roused the thought of study. I consulted my cousin Shen Cheng, who said: 'Mr. Yu Haigu is teaching at the home of Shen Youfu; I will send you to board there, which is very convenient.' So I paid my respects to Yu as my teacher.

Kong cast my numbers: in the county examination among the students I should be fourteenth; in the prefectural examination seventy-first; in the education commissioner's examination ninth. The next year I sat for the examinations, and the numbers in all three places matched.

He further divined the fortune of my whole life, saying: 'In such a year you will be ranked such a number; in such a year you should receive the government stipend; in such a year you should become a tribute student; after becoming a tribute student, in such a year you should be selected as a magistrate of Sichuan; after three and a half years in office, you should at once retire. On the fourteenth day of the eighth month in your fifty-third year, at the hour of the ox, you will die in your own bed, but alas you will have no son.' I recorded it all and carefully remembered it.

From then on, whenever I was examined, the order of my names never fell outside what Master Kong had fixed. Only he calculated that my stipended rice should amount to ninety-one dan and five dou before I became a tribute student; but when the rice reached seventy-something dan, Examiner Tu approved my promotion to tribute student, and I secretly doubted it. Later it was indeed rejected by the acting seal-holder, Mr. Yang.
Until the year of Dingmao (when Master Liaofan was

years old), Examiner Yin Qiuming, seeing my reserve examination papers, sighed: 'These five policy essays are five memorials to the throne. How can a scholar so broad and thorough be left to grow old beneath his window!' So he approved my tributeship according to the county's recommendation, and counting the previous rice, it came truly to ninety-one dan and five dou.

I therefore believed all the more that 'advancement and retreat are destined, and speed and delay have their time,' and became tranquil and without longing. After becoming a tribute student I entered the capital, Yanjing, and stayed a year, sitting in stillness all day and not reading a single text.
In the year Jisi (when Master Liaofan was

years old) I returned and traveled to the Southern College. Before entering, I first visited Yungu, meeting the Chan master in Mount Qixia. We sat facing each other in one room for three days and nights without closing our eyes. Yungu asked: 'The reason ordinary people cannot become sages is only that they are tangled in false thoughts. You have sat three days without producing a single false thought. Why is that?' I said: 'My fate was fixed by Master Kong; honor and disgrace, life and death all have their fixed number. Even if I wished to have false thoughts, I could not.'

Yungu laughed and said: 'I took you for a hero, but you are only an ordinary man!' Asked why, he said: 'A person who cannot be without a mind is ultimately bound by yin and yang; how can there be no fate? But only ordinary people have a fixed fate. For the extremely good, fate cannot bind him; for the extremely evil, fate also cannot bind him. For these twenty years you have been bound by his calculations without moving a hair. Is that not to be an ordinary man?'

I asked: 'Then can fate be escaped?' He said: 'Destiny is made by oneself; blessing is sought from oneself.' What the Book of Songs and the Book of History say is indeed a clear teaching. In my teaching it says: 'Seek wealth and you get wealth; seek a son and you get a son; seek long life and you get long life.' False speech is the great precept of Śākyamuni; how could the Buddhas and bodhisattvas deceive people with lies?'
I pressed on: 'Mencius says: 'Seek and you get it; this is seeking within myself.' Moral virtue and benevolence can be sought with effort; but how can fame, rank, wealth, and honor be sought?'

Yungu said: 'Mencius' words are not wrong; it is you who have misunderstood. Do you not see the Sixth Patriarch's saying: 'All fields of blessing are not separate from the square inch of the mind; seeking from the mind, nothing is unattainable.' Seeking in oneself, one gains not only moral virtue and benevolence but also fame, rank, wealth, and honor, obtaining both the inner and the outer; this is seeking that profits the attainment. If one does not reflect within but only rushes outward in pursuit, then though one seeks by a way, the attainment is still fixed by fate; one loses both the inner and the outer, and so it is of no benefit.'

He then asked: 'What did Master Kong calculate for your whole life?' I told him truthfully. Yungu said: 'Do you judge for yourself whether you should obtain the rank of the examinations? Should you have a son?'

I reflected a long while and said: 'No, I should not. Those of the examination ranks generally have the appearance of fortune. My fortune is thin, and I cannot accumulate merit and virtue to found a thick fortune; moreover I cannot endure complexity, cannot tolerate others, sometimes I use my talents to outdo others, and act straightforwardly, speaking triflingly and rashly. All these are signs of a thin fortune. How could I deserve the examinations!'

The filthy earth produces growing things, while the clearest water often has no fish. My love of cleanliness is the first reason I should have no son. Harmony can nurture all things; I am prone to anger, the second reason. Compassion is the root of life; harshness is the root of its absence. I cling to my reputation and often cannot give up myself to save others, the third reason. Much speech wastes breath, the fourth reason. Fondness for drink burns away essence, the fifth reason. I love to sit through the night without knowing to conserve the primal and nurture the spirit, the sixth reason. There are yet many other faults and evils, too many to list fully.'

Yungu said: 'Is it only the examinations! Those who enjoy a thousand pieces of gold in the world are surely persons of a thousand pieces of gold; those who enjoy a hundred pieces are surely persons of a hundred pieces; those who should die of hunger are surely people who die of hunger. Heaven merely is sincere according to the substance; how much thought did it ever add?

So with begetting a son: one with a hundred generations of virtue surely has descendants who protect it for a hundred generations; one with ten generations of virtue surely has descendants who protect it for ten generations; one with three generations or two generations of virtue surely has descendants who protect it for three or two generations; and the one cut off with no descendants is one whose virtue is thin.'

Now that you know your faults, you should completely reform the appearances that kept you from passing the examinations and from having a son. Be sure to accumulate virtue, be sure to be tolerant, be sure to be loving, be sure to cherish the spirit. Whatever was before, let it be as though you died yesterday. Whatever comes after, let it be as though you were born today. This is the body reborn through principle and righteousness.'

The body of flesh and blood is still subject to fate; how could the body of principle and righteousness not move heaven? Taijia says: 'The calamity Heaven makes can still be avoided; the calamity one makes for oneself cannot be survived.' The Book of Songs says: 'Always accord with Heaven's decree and seek your own blessing.' Master Kong calculated that you would not pass the examinations and would not have a son; this is the calamity Heaven makes, and it can still be avoided. Now if you expand your virtue, practice good deeds diligently, and accumulate hidden merit, this is the blessing you make for yourself; how could you fail to enjoy it?'

The Book of Changes plans for the gentleman, moving toward good fortune and away from calamity. If the decree of Heaven were unchangeable, how could good fortune be approached or calamity avoided? In the very first principle it says: 'The household that accumulates goodness is sure to have abundant joy.' Can you believe this?'

I believed his words and bowed to receive his instruction. I thereupon confessed all my past faults fully before the Buddha, writing a prayer, first seeking to pass the examinations, and vowing to practice three thousand good deeds to repay the virtue of heaven, earth, and my ancestors.

Yungu brought out the ledger of merit and demerit and showed it to me, telling me to record every day what I did, counting good deeds and deducting evil ones. He also taught me to hold the mantra of Cundi, so as to be sure of success.

He said to me: 'The talisman masters say: 'If you cannot write a talisman, the spirits and ghosts will laugh at you.' This has a secret transmission, which is simply not to move the mind. When you take up the brush to write a talisman, first put down all conditions of the ten thousand things, so that not one particle of dust arises. From this, at the place where the thought does not move, you place a dot; this is called opening the foundation of chaos. From there, in one stroke it is completed, without further deliberation, and the talisman becomes efficacious. All who pray to Heaven to establish their destiny must raise the response from the place free of thought and deliberation.

Mencius, discussing the study of establishing destiny, says: 'Early and late death are not two.' Now early death and long life are the most divided things! At the time the thought does not move, what is early death and what is long life? When broken down further, when abundance and want are not two, then one can establish the destiny of wealth and poverty; when success and failure are not two, then one can establish the destiny of nobility and lowliness; when early death and long life are not two, then one can establish the destiny of life and death. In human life in this world, life and death alone are most important; and when early death and long life are included, all favourable and adverse circumstances are encompassed within them.'

As for cultivating oneself to await the decree, this is the task of accumulating virtue and praying to Heaven. 'Cultivate' means that the faults and evils of the body should all be corrected and removed; 'await' means that a single thought of coveting or anticipating should all be cut off. Arriving at this state, one directly enters the realm of the primal. This is true learning!'

You cannot yet be without a mind, but you can hold the mantra of Cundi. Count it without number, and do not let it be interrupted. When you have held it so that it is utterly familiar, and within the holding there is no holding, and within the not-holding there is holding, until the thought does not move, then it becomes efficacious.'
My original style name was Xuehai; on that day I changed it to Liaofan, because I had awakened to the teaching of establishing destiny and did not wish to fall into the ruts of an ordinary man.

From then on, I was diligent all day and felt differently from before. Earlier I had been drifting and at ease; now I felt a state of trembling and watchfulness. Even in a dark room and a leaky house, I always feared offending heaven, earth, ghosts, and spirits. When others disliked and slandered me, I could myself peacefully accept it.

The next year, in the Ministry of Rites examination for the provincial degree, Master Kong had calculated that I should be third; unexpectedly I was first, and his words did not hold, and I passed the provincial examination.

Yet my practice of righteousness was not pure, and I often erred in examining myself. Sometimes I saw a good deed but did not do it bravely; sometimes I saved someone but my heart still doubted; sometimes I strove to do good but my mouth spoke overhastily; sometimes I upheld myself while awake but let go in drunkenness. Offenses offsetting merit, my days were spent in idleness.
From the year Jisi when I made the vow, until the year Jimao (when I was

years old), after more than ten years, the three thousand good deeds were finally completed. At that time I was just entering the pass with Li Jian'an, and had not yet dedicated the merit; in the year Gengchen (when I was
years old) I returned south, and only then invited the venerables Xingkong and Huikong to dedicate it in the East Pagoda Chan Hall.
I then made the vow to seek a son, and also promised to practice three thousand good deeds. In the year Xinsi (when I was

years old), a son was born, Tianqi. Each time I did a good deed I recorded it in writing; my wife could not write, so each time she did a good deed she used a goose-feather tube to stamp a red circle on the calendar, whether giving food to the poor or buying and releasing living creatures, sometimes reaching more than ten circles in a single day. By the eighth month of the year Guiwei (when I was
years old), the three thousand were complete. I invited Xingkong and the others again to dedicate it at home.
On the thirteenth day of the ninth month, I made the vow to seek passing the highest examination, promising to practice ten thousand good deeds. In the year Bingxu (when I was

years old) I passed and was appointed magistrate of Baodi. I kept a blank ledger named 'The Compilation of Mind-Cultivation.' In the morning when I took my seat in the hall, my family handed it to the gate officer, who placed it on the table; whatever good or evil I did, I recorded it in full detail. At night I set a table in the courtyard and, following Zhao Yuedao, burned incense and reported to the Emperor.

My wife, seeing that the good deeds were many but few, knit her brows and said: 'Before, at home I helped in doing good, so the three thousand were completed; now you have promised ten thousand, and in the yamen office there is nothing to do. When will it be fulfilled?' That night I happened to dream of a spirit, and I told him my difficulty in completing the good deeds. The spirit said: 'Only the single matter of reducing the grain levy completes all ten thousand deeds.' For the fields of Baodi, the levy was two fen, three li, and seven ha per mu; I made arrangements and reduced it to one fen, four li, and six ha. Since this was indeed the case, my heart was rather startled and doubtful.

Just then Chan Master Huanyu came from Mount Wutai, and I told him my dream and asked whether the matter should be believed. The master said: 'When the good heart is genuine, a single deed can serve as ten thousand good deeds, and this is all the more so when reducing the grain levy for the whole county benefits ten thousand people!' I thereupon donated the silver of my salary and asked him to go to Mount Wutai and feed the monks for ten thousand toward the dedication of merit.
Master Kong calculated that in my fifty-third year there would be a calamity; I never prayed for long life, yet that year I was unharmed, and now I am sixty-nine.

The Book of History says: 'Heaven is hard to trust; the mandate is not constant.' It also says: 'The mandate alone is not fixed.' None of these is false speech. From this I know that those who say blessing and calamity are sought from oneself speak the words of sages; but those who say blessing and calamity are alone decreed by Heaven speak the common talk of the world.

Your destiny is unknown. Even if it is destined for honor and glory, always think of obscurity; even when times are smooth, always think of adversity; even if you are well fed before your eyes, always think of poverty; even if people love and respect you, always think with fear; even if your family name is honored, always think of lowliness; even if your learning is excellent, always think of shallowness.

Thinking far, extol the virtue of your ancestors; thinking near, cover the faults of your parents; thinking upward, repay the grace of the state; thinking downward, create the blessing of the family; thinking outward, relieve the urgent needs of others; thinking inward, guard against your own evil.

Be sure to know your faults every day and reform them every day. If one day you do not know your faults, you are content with yourself for a day; if one day you have no fault to correct, you have made no progress for a day. The world is not lacking in clever and handsome people; the reason their virtue is not cultivated and their work is not broadened is only the two words of procrastination, which ruining a whole life.
The teaching of establishing destiny given by Chan Master Yungu is a principle of extreme refinement, profundity, truth, and correctness. Ruminate on it and practice it diligently; do not neglect it.

blocks.text: The Second Teaching: The Method of Reforming Faults

inline.s: The great officers of the Spring and Autumn period, seeing a person's speech and actions, conjectured and spoke of his fortune and misfortune, and none failed to be verified; the records of the Zuo Commentary and the Guoyu can be seen. For the most part, the omens of good fortune and calamity arise in the mind and move through the four limbs. Those who are too generous receive good fortune; those who are too mean approach calamity. The common eye is much clouded, thinking these unascertainable and unmeasurable. But when utmost sincerity accords with Heaven, when good fortune is about to come, seeing his goodness one must know of it beforehand; when calamity is about to come, seeing his evil one must know of it beforehand.

blocks.text: 1. The Three Minds of Reforming Faults

inline.s: Now to obtain good fortune and stay far from calamity, before speaking of doing good, one must first reform one's faults. But those who reform their faults:
First, one must arouse the mind of shame.
Think of the sages of old, who were men like me. How is it they can be the teachers of a hundred generations, while I am as a single brick shattered to pieces?

Immersing oneself in worldly passions and secretly doing what is unjust, thinking no one knows, and being prideful without shame, one sinks daily toward the beasts without knowing it. Of the things in the world to be ashamed of, none is greater than this! Mencius says: 'Shame is of great importance to a person.' Because one who has it becomes a sage, and one who loses it becomes a beast. This is the crucial point of reforming faults.
Second, one must arouse the mind of reverence.

Heaven and earth are above; ghosts and spirits cannot be deceived. Though my faults are hidden and subtle, heaven, earth, ghosts, and spirits truly look upon them. For grave ones they send down a hundred calamities; for light ones they diminish one's present fortune. How can I not fear?

Not only that. In a place of idleness, the pointing eyes are manifest. Though I cover it closely and dress it cleverly, my very heart and liver are already exposed, and in the end it is hard to deceive myself; once seen through by others, it is not worth a cent! How can one not be fearful?

Not only that. While a single breath remains, the greatest wickedness of a whole life may still be repented. The ancients have those who did evil all their lives and repented at death, giving rise to a single good thought, and so came to a good end; this is a single fierce thought sufficient to wash away a hundred years of evil. Like a thousand-year dark valley: at the moment a lamp shines, the darkness of a thousand years is all dispelled. Therefore faults, whether recent or ancient, are precious only in being reformed. But the world is impermanent and the body easily perishes; when the breath no longer belongs to one, one has no way to reform. While alive one bears the name of evil for a hundred generations, and even filial sons and loving grandsons cannot wash it away; in the dark one sinks into the retribution of the prison for a hundred kalpas, and even sages and Buddhas cannot rescue one. How can one not fear?
Third, one must arouse the mind of courage.

People who do not reform their faults are mostly procrastinating and shrinking. I must rouse myself and act, without hesitation and without waiting. For small faults like a thorn in the flesh, quickly pluck it out; for great faults like a poisonous snake biting the finger, quickly cut it off. Without the slightest hesitation, this is why wind and thunder are of benefit.
With these three minds, then faults are reformed wherever found, like spring ice meeting the sun; how could one worry that it will not melt?

blocks.text: 2. The Three Methods of Reforming Faults

inline.s: But human faults may be reformed on the level of the matter, or on the level of principle, or on the level of the mind; the effort differs, and the results differ too.

As yesterday you killed living beings, today you vow not to kill; yesterday you scolded in anger, today you vow not to be angry; this is reforming on the level of the deed. Forcefully restraining oneself externally is a hundred times harder, and the root of the disease remains in the end; quenched in the east it arises in the west, and so it is not the way of ultimate clarity.

The good reformer of faults, before prohibiting the deed, first understands the principle. If the fault lies in killing, then reflect: Heaven delights in life, and all things cling to life. To kill them to nourish myself, how can I be at ease? Moreover, when they are killed, they suffer the butcher's knife and enter the boiling cauldron, all kinds of pain penetrating to the marrow; while my own nourishment, delicacies set in array, becomes nothing after eating, whereas plain food and vegetable broth are quite enough to fill the belly. Why must I destroy their lives and diminish my own fortune?

Again reflect: all creatures of blood and breath contain spirit and awareness; since they have spirit and awareness, they are one with me. Even if I cannot cultivate supreme virtue so that they revere and befriend me, how can I daily destroy their lives so that they hate me and resent me without end? At the thought of this, one will face food with sadness and be unable to swallow.

As yesterday you were prone to anger, reflect: where people are deficient, it is natural to feel compassion; when they violate principle and oppose me, what has it to do with me? There is fundamentally nothing to be angry about. Again reflect: there is no self-righteous hero in the world, and no learning that blames others. When one's conduct does not attain its goal, it is because one's virtue is not cultivated and one's influence has not arrived. Using all this to turn upon myself, slander and blame when they come are places to temper and perfect me; I will joyfully receive the gift, and what anger would there be? Moreover, if one hears slander and does not get angry, though the flames of calumny blaze to the heavens, it is like lighting a fire to burn the sky, which in the end dies of itself. If one hears slander and grows angry, though one uses clever words to defend, it is like a spring silkworm making its cocoon, entangling itself; anger is not only useless but also harmful.
As for the remaining various faults and evils, one should all reflect upon them according to principle. Once this principle is clear, the faults will stop of themselves.

What does reform from within the mind mean? Faults have a thousand ends, but are all made by the mind; if my mind does not move, where can faults arise? The student, with respect to the various faults of loving beauty, loving fame, loving wealth, loving anger, need not seek them out one by one by kind; only by making the mind single in goodness, so that the right thought appears before him, will the evil thought naturally find no way to defile it. As when the sun is in the sky, the goblins vanish of themselves; this is the true transmission of refined unity! Faults are made by the mind and also reformed by the mind, as with cutting a poison tree, one cuts straight through its root; why must one prune branch by branch and pluck leaf by leaf?

Broadly speaking, the highest practice is to govern the mind, so that it is pure and clear in the present moment; as soon as a thought stirs, one is aware of it, and once aware, it is gone. If one cannot yet do this, one must clarify principle so as to dispel the thought; and if one cannot yet do that, one must restrain it in accordance with circumstances. To practice the higher method while also carrying out the lower exercises is not a misstep; but to cling to the lower and remain ignorant of the higher is clumsy indeed.

Now when one makes a vow to correct one's faults, in the open daylight one needs good friends to remind him, and in the hidden dark one needs gods and spirits to bear witness. With a single mind he repents, night and day without slacking, and after a week, two weeks, on to a month, two months, three months, there is sure to be an effect. He may feel his mind and spirit tranquil and open; or feel his wisdom suddenly opened; or amid pressing affairs find every thought meeting with ease; or meeting a foe, have his anger turn to joy; or dream of vomiting black things; or dream of the sages of old coming to lead and guide him; or dream of striding through the great void; or dream of banners and jeweled canopies. These various auspicious occurrences are all signs that his faults have dissolved and his offenses extinguished.

Yet one must not grasp at these and think highly of oneself, halting and making no progress. In former days, when Qu Boyu was twenty, he already felt the errors of the day before and corrected them all; by twenty-one he knew that what he had corrected was not yet complete; and at twenty-two, looking back on twenty-one, it was as though he had still been dreaming. Year after year he went on changing, and when he was fifty he still knew the errors of his forty-ninth year. Such was the learning of correcting faults among the ancients! We are of the common run, and our faults and evils gather like hedgehogs; yet when we look back on the past, we often seem to see no fault in ourselves — because our minds are coarse and our eyes clouded.

But for those whose faults and evils are deep and heavy, there are also effects: the mind and spirit are clouded and blocked, so that one forgets as soon as one turns one's head; or one is often vexed without any cause; or one flushes and withers when meeting a noble man; or one is displeased upon hearing right discussion; or one bestows kindness and is repaid with resentment; or one dreams wildly and confusedly, or even speaks wildly and loses his resolve — these are all signs of having wrought harm. If one sees even a single one of these, he must arouse himself, abandon the old and seek the new; pray do not wrong yourself!

blocks.text: Part Three. The Method of Accumulating Goodness

inline.s: The Book of Changes says, “A family that accumulates goodness will surely have an abundance of happiness.” In former days the Yan family was about to give its daughter in marriage to Shulianghe, and told in detail of his ancestors' long accumulation of virtue, foreknowing that his descendants would surely have those who would rise. Confucius, praising the great filial piety of Shun, said, “The ancestral temple will feast him, and his descendants will preserve it.” These are all profound sayings. Let us test them by past events:

Yang Rong, the Junior Preceptor, was a man of Jianning, whose family for generations made their living by ferrying people across the river. After a long rain the stream swelled, and the flood rushed across and destroyed the houses of the people, so that those who drowned swept along with the current. The other boats all snatched at the goods; only the Junior Preceptor's great-grandfather and grandfather rescued people and took nothing of the cargo, and the villagers laughed at their folly. When the Junior Preceptor's father was born, the family gradually grew prosperous. A divine being, transformed into a Taoist, said to him, “Your grandfather and great-grandfather have hidden merit; their descendants ought to become noble and honored, and you should bury them in such and such a place.” So he followed his direction and buried them there; this is the present White Rabbit Tomb. Later the Junior Preceptor was born, and at twenty he passed the examinations and rose to the rank of the Three Dukes, and his great-grandfather, grandfather, and father were given the same ranks. His descendants were rich and honored, and to this day there are many worthy men among them.

Yang Zicheng of Yin was at first a county clerk, but his heart was kind and benevolent and he kept the law fair and even. At that time the magistrate was stern and severe, and once beat a prisoner until the blood flowed over the floor while his anger was still unappeased. Yang knelt and pleaded to soothe him. The magistrate said, “What can one do? This man has overstepped the law and defied all principle; how can I not be angry?” Zicheng kowtowed and said, “When those above have lost the way, the people have been scattered for a long time. If one gets at the truth of a case, one should pity them and not rejoice; if rejoicing is not right, how much more anger?” The magistrate thereupon relaxed his countenance. Yang's family was very poor, and he accepted nothing that was given to him. Whenever prisoners lacked food, he would in many ways help them.

One day several new prisoners were waiting to be fed, and the family again lacked rice. If he gave to the prisoners, his own family would have nothing to eat; if he looked to his own, the prisoners were pitiable. He consulted with his wife, and she said, “Where do the prisoners come from?” He said, “They come from Hangzhou. Along the way they have gone hungry, and their faces are as green as can be.” So he took from his own rice and boiled gruel to feed the prisoners.

Afterwards two sons were born to him; the elder was named Shouchen and the younger Shouzhi, and they became vice-ministers of the Board of Personnel for the south and the north. His eldest grandson was a vice-minister of the Board of Punishments, and the second grandson was the commissioner of Sichuan. They were all famous ministers; and Chuting and Dezheng of today are also his descendants.

In the days of Zhengtong, Deng Maoqi raised a rebellion in Fujian, and very many scholars and common people joined the rebels. The court sent the censor-in-chief Zhang Kai of Yin county to march south and take the rebels with a stratagem, and then committed to the administration commissioner Xie the task of hunting down the rebel bands of the eastern route. Xie sought the registers of those who had joined the rebels, and to all who had not joined he secretly gave little flags of white cloth, telling them to plant the flags at their doors on the day the soldiers arrived; and he ordered the troops not to kill indiscriminately. In this way tens of thousands were saved alive. Later Xie's son Qian came in first in the examinations and became a chief minister; his grandson Pi came in third.

The Lin family of Putian: in former generations an old mother loved to do good, and would often make rice-flour balls to give to people; whoever asked for them she gave them to without any sign of weariness. An immortal, transformed into a Taoist, would every morning beg six or seven balls; the mother gave them every day, for three years without a break, and only then did he know her sincerity. So he said to her, “I have eaten your rice-flour balls for three years; how shall I repay you? Behind your house there is a piece of ground; if you bury there, your descendants' ranks and offices will be as numerous as a sheng of sesame seeds.” Her son buried his parents in the place he pointed out, and in the very first generation nine men passed the examinations, and generation after generation of officials was very flourishing, so that in Fujian there went about the saying, “Without the Lins, no roll is opened.”

The father of Feng Zhuoan, the historiographer, was a county student. One winter morning very early he rose and set out for his school, and on the way met a man lying fallen in the snow; when he touched him, he was half frozen. So he undid his own padded coat and covered him with it, and carried him home and revived him. He dreamed that a god told him, “You have saved a man's life out of a most sincere heart; I will send Han Qi to be your son.” When Zhuoan was born, he thereupon named him Qi.

Minister Ying of Taizhou, when he was young, studied in the mountains. At night the ghosts would gather and howl and often frighten people, but Ying was not afraid. One evening he heard a ghost say, “A certain woman, because her husband has long been away and does not return, is being pressed by her parents-in-law to marry another; tomorrow night she will hang herself here, and I shall gain my replacement.” Ying secretly sold some land and got four taels of silver, then forged a letter in her husband's hand and sent the silver home. When her parents saw the letter, they suspected it because the hand was not like his, but then said, “The letter may be false, but the silver cannot be false; the boy must be well.” The woman therefore did not remarry. Later her husband returned, and the couple were preserved together as before.

Ying again heard a ghost say, “I was to get my replacement, but this scholar has spoilt my affair.” Another ghost beside it said, “Why not bring misfortune on him?” The first said, “Heaven regards this man's heart as good and has appointed him to be a minister of hidden virtue; how can I bring misfortune on him?” Because of this Ying grew the more diligent, cultivating goodness day by day and deepening his virtue day by day. When the harvest failed, he would give grain to relieve the people; when relatives were in need, he would arrange matters to support them; and when he met with contumely and outrage, he would turn and reproach himself, accepting it calmly. His descendants who have passed the examinations are, even today, many.

Xu Fengzhu (Shen) of Changshu — his father was always wealthy. Once he happened upon a famine year, and was the first in his county to release the rents, and then divided grain to relieve the poor. At night he heard ghosts singing at the gate: “Not a thousand lies, not ten thousand lies, the Xu family's scholar has become a provincial graduate!” Repeatedly and continuously they called through the night without stopping; that year Fengzhu indeed was selected in the provincial examinations. His father thereby accumulated more virtue, diligent without rest, repairing bridges and roads, feeding monks and welcoming the throng; and in whatever was beneficial he gave his whole heart. Later again he heard the ghosts singing at the gate: “Not a thousand lies, not ten thousand lies, the Xu family's graduate rises straight to the censorate.” Fengzhu ended his office as governor-general of the Two Zhe.

Tu Kangxi of Jiaxing, when first a secretary of the Board of Punishments, lodged in the prison and questioned the prisoners one by one about their circumstances, and found several who were innocent. He did not take credit for it himself, but privately wrote up the matter and reported it to the president of the board. Later at the autumn assizes the president used his words to examine the prisoners, and there was not one who was not convinced; more than ten were released from wrongful imprisonment. For a time all the capital praised the minister's perspicacity.

Ying again reported, “Beneath the wheels of the capital there are still many wronged people; in the breadth of the four seas, among the multitudes of millions, how could there be none who are wronged? We should every five years send out a commissioner to reduce sentences, to verify and reverse them.” The minister memorialized the proposal and it was approved; and Ying was also among those sent to reduce sentences. He dreamed a god told him, “You are destined to have no son; but this proposal to reduce sentences deeply accords with Heaven's heart, and Heaven will grant you three sons, all wearing purple and girded with gold.” That night his wife conceived, and afterwards gave birth to Yingxun, Yingkun, and Yingling, all of whom became high officials.

Bao Ping of Jiaxing, style Xinzhi, had a father who was the prefect of Chiyang. He had seven sons, and Ping was the youngest; he married into the Yuan family of Pinghu and had close dealings with my father. Learned and highly talented, he sat for the examinations repeatedly without success, and turned his attention to the teachings of the two schools. One day he journeyed east to Maohu lake, and happened upon a village temple where he saw a Guanyin image standing exposed in the rain. He at once opened his purse and got ten taels of gold, which he gave to the abbot, telling him to repair the building. The monk told him the work was great and the silver little, and that he could not complete it. Ping took again four bolts of loose silk and seven garments from his trunk and gave them to him; among them a new robe of arame, which his servant asked him to keep. Ping said, “So long as the holy image is unharmed, what matter if I go naked?” The monk wept and said, “To give up silver, clothes and silk is not so hard; but this single point of heart — how hard it is to get!” When the work was done, he brought his old father along to tour the place, and they lodged in the temple. Ping dreamed the temple guardian came to thank him, saying, “Your son shall enjoy the emoluments of the world.” Later his son Bian and grandson Chengfang both passed the examinations and became high officials.

The father of Zhi Li of Jiashan was a clerk in the penal office. There was a prisoner who was innocent but had fallen into a capital sentence, and he, pitying him, wished to save his life. The prisoner said to his wife, “Master Zhi has kind intentions, and I am ashamed that I have nothing to repay him. Tomorrow invite him into the country; serve him with your body; if he will perhaps be willing to use his efforts on my behalf, then I may live.” His wife wept and obeyed. When he came, the wife herself came out to urge the wine and told him fully of her husband's intent. Zhi refused, and in the end did his utmost to clear and reverse the case.

When the prisoner came out of prison, the husband and wife came to his gate to kowtow their thanks, saying, “Your kindness, sir, is so great that it is rare in this late age. You now have no son; we have a young daughter, and we give her to you as a slave-concubine; this is what the rites permit.” Zhi accepted her with proper rites, and a son was born named Li, who at twenty won first place in the examinations and became a secretary of the Hanlin Academy; Li bore Gao, and Gao bore Lu, all of whom were sent up as learned teachers; and Lu bore Dalun, who passed the examinations.

blocks.text: 2. The Eight Distinctions of Practicing Goodness

inline.s: These ten examples differ in what they did, but all alike return to goodness. If we speak of it more precisely, however, goodness has the true and the false, the upright and the crooked, the secret and the open, the right and the wrong, the partial and the correct, the half and the full, the great and the small, the hard and the easy — all of which should be deeply distinguished. If one does good without exhausting principle, he thinks he is in practice, yet he knows not that he is making mischief, and is wasting his pains to no benefit.
What is meant by true and false?

In former days several Confucian scholars went to consult the Zen master Zhongfeng, and asked, “The Buddha's teaching speaks of reward and retribution for good and evil as following like a shadow. Now one man is good, yet his descendants do not flourish; another is evil, yet his whole house is prosperous — so the Buddha's words are groundless!” Zhongfeng said, “The vulgar feelings of the ordinary man have not been washed away, and his true eye is not yet opened; to take good for evil and evil for good happens often enough. Do you not grieve at the inversion of right and wrong in your own hearts, and yet turn your resentment upon Heaven's reward and retribution for being amiss?” The men said, “How should good and evil be thus reversed?” Zhongfeng bade them each say what they thought. One said, “To curse a man and strike a man is evil; to respect a man and salute a man is good.” Zhongfeng said, “Not necessarily.” Another said, “To be greedy for wealth and take wrongly is evil; to be clean and self-restrained is good.” Zhongfeng said, “Not necessarily.”

The men told out their cases one by one, and Zhongfeng said that none were necessarily so. So they asked him, and Zhongfeng told them, “What benefits others is good; what benefits oneself is evil. If it benefits others, then to strike a man and curse a man are both good; if it benefits oneself, then to respect a man and salute a man are both evil. Thus, when a man does good, he who benefits others is public-spirited, and being public-spirited is true; he who benefits himself is selfish, and being selfish is false. Again, what springs from the root of the heart is true; what merely imitates the outward trace is false. Again, what is done without contrivance is true; what is done with contrivance is false. All should be examined in oneself.”
What is meant by upright and crooked?

Today people see a prudent, well-meaning man and generally praise him as good and so take to him; but the sage rather takes the bold and the self-willed. As for the prudent, well-meaning man, though the whole village likes him, the sage must regard him as the thief of virtue — so the world's good and evil are plainly the reverse of the sage's. Pushing this one point further, in every sort of choice and rejection there is no error that is not committed; and Heaven, Earth, gods and spirits bless the good and afflict the licentious in the same right and wrong as the sage, not at all sharing the world's choice and rejection. Whoever would accumulate goodness must by no means follow his ears and eyes, but from the hidden place at the root of the mind silently wash himself clean. If it is wholly a heart of saving the world, it is upright; if there is the slightest trace of courtly flattery, it is crooked. If it is wholly a heart of loving others, it is upright; if there is the slightest trace of hatred of the age, it is crooked. If it is wholly a heart of respecting others, it is upright; if there is the slightest trace of making sport of the world, it is crooked. All should be finely distinguished.
What is meant by secret and open?

Whenever one does good and others know of it, it is called open goodness; when one does good and others do not know of it, it is called hidden virtue. Hidden virtue is rewarded by Heaven; open goodness enjoys a name in the world, and a name is a blessing too. But a name is what the Creator envies. Those in the world who enjoy a great name that they do not really match often meet with strange calamities; while men who are without fault yet are slandered with a bad name find their descendants suddenly rise. Oh, the boundary between hidden and open is subtle indeed!
What is meant by right and wrong?

The law of Lu was that if a man of Lu redeemed a fellow-countryman who had been taken as a subject or concubine by the feudal lords, he received the price from the treasury. Zigong redeemed a man but would not accept the money, and when Confucius heard of it he disapproved, saying, “Ci has erred! When the sage initiates a matter, it is to change the manners and customs of the age, and the teaching can be applied to the common people, not merely to suit his own conduct. Now in Lu the rich are few and the poor many; if to accept the money is to be regarded as unprincipled, then how shall men redeem each other? From now on, no one will redeem people from the feudal lords again!”
Zilu rescued a man from drowning, and the man thanked him with an ox, and Zilu accepted it. Confucius was pleased and said, “From now on the men of Lu will rescue many from drowning!”

Seen through the vulgar eye, Zigong's not accepting the money seems superior and Zilu's accepting the ox seems inferior; but Confucius took Zilu's side and dismissed Zigong. From this we learn that in doing good one does not judge by the present act but by the flowing consequences; not by the moment but by the long ages; not by one's own case but by the whole world. If the present act is good but its consequences are enough to harm men, then it is seemingly good but really not; if the present act is not good but its consequences are enough to help men, then it is seemingly not good but really is. Yet this is to speak of a single case only. Other things, as the righteousness that is not righteous, the propriety that is not proper, the trust that is not trustworthy, and the compassion that is not compassionate — all should be judged likewise.
What is meant by partial and correct?

In former days Lord Lu Wenyi, having just resigned the rank of premier, returned to his home village, and the whole world looked up to him as to Mount Tai and the Northern Pole. A village fellow, drunk, cursed him; Lu gave no response, but said to his servants, “Do not contend with a drunkard; shut the gate and be done with him.” A year later the man committed a capital crime and was thrown into prison, and Lu at last regretted it, saying, “Had I at the time made the least reckoning with him and sent him to the authorities to be punished, a small chastisement might have been a great warning. I only wished to preserve my heart in generosity, and did not expect that I would nourish his wickedness until it came to this!” This is a case of doing an evil deed with a good heart.

There is also the doing of good deeds with an evil heart. For example: a certain family was very rich, and a famine year came; the poor openly snatched grain from the market in broad daylight. He reported it to the county, but the county would not act, and the poor grew bolder. So he seized them himself and bound and shamed them, and the crowd settled down only then; otherwise there would almost have been a riot.

Thus good is correct and evil is partial, as everyone knows. But doing an evil deed with a good heart is the correct within the partial; doing a good deed with an evil heart is the partial within the correct. One must not fail to understand this.
What is meant by half and full?

The Book of Changes says, “Goodness, unless accumulated, is not enough to establish a name; evil, unless accumulated, is not enough to destroy one's life.” The Book of History says, “The offenses of Shang are full to overflowing.” It is like storing things in a vessel: if you diligently keep adding to it, it becomes full; if you slacken and do not add, it does not fill. This is one way of saying it.

In former days a certain daughter of a family went into a temple and, wishing to give alms but having no wealth, had only two cash; she gave them, and the abbot in person performed the confession for her. Later she entered the palace and became rich and honored, and took several thousand cash into the temple to give; but the abbot only had a disciple offer the merit for her. So she asked, “Formerly when I gave two cash, you yourself performed the confession; now I give several thousand, and you do not offer the merit. Why?” He said, “In the former case, though the gift was small, the heart of giving was most sincere; had I not in person confessed it, it would not have been enough to repay the virtue. Now, though the gift is great, the heart of giving is not as earnest as before; to have another offer the merit for you is enough.” So the several thousand were but half, and the two cash were full.

Zhongli transmitted the elixir to the Ancestor Lu, touching iron to turn it to gold, so as to save the world. Lu asked, “Will it ever change again?” Zhongli said, “After five hundred years it will return to its original substance.” Lu said, “If so, it would do harm to the people of five hundred years hence; I would not do it.” Zhongli said, “To cultivate immortality one must accumulate three thousand deeds of merit. That one word of yours has already fulfilled the three thousand deeds of merit.” This is another way of saying it.

Again, when one does good and the heart does not dwell on the good, then whatever is accomplished is all perfect; but if the heart dwells on the good, then though one strive hard a whole lifetime, it remains only half-good. For example, in using wealth to help others, if within one does not see oneself, without one does not see others, and in the middle one does not see the thing given, this is called the threefold wheel of giving being empty, and is called a single-minded purity; then a single peck of grain can plant boundless blessing, and a single cash can extinguish the offenses of a thousand eons. But if this heart is not forgotten, though the gold be ten thousand yi, the blessing is not full. This is yet another way of saying it.
What is meant by great and small?

In former days Wei Zhongda held an office in the academies, and was seized and carried off to the underworld; the ruler of that realm ordered the clerks to bring up the two registers of his good and evil. When they came, the register of evil filled the whole hall, while the register of good was but a single scroll, as slender as a chopstick. When they were weighed on the scales, the one that filled the hall was the lighter, and the one like a chopstick was the heavier. Zhongda said, “I am not yet forty; how can my offenses be so many?” He was told, “A single thought that is not right is counted; there is no need to have committed it.” He asked what was written on the scroll, and was told, “Once the court raised a great undertaking to build the three-mountain stone bridge, and you submitted a memorial advising against it; this is the draft of that memorial.” Zhongda said, “Though I spoke, the court did not follow me, and it availed nothing; how could it have such power?” He was told, “Though the court did not follow, your single thought was already for the myriad people; if it had followed, the power of the goodness would have been even greater.” Therefore, if the resolve be for the realm and the state, then though the good be small it is great; if it be for one's own person, then though it be much it is small.
What is meant by hard and easy?

The former Confucians said, “In overcoming oneself, one must overcome it at the place where it is hardest to overcome.” The Master, discussing “practicing humanity,” also said, “Begin with the hard.” So it must be like the elder Shu of Jiangxi, who gave the two years' worth of his modest teaching fees that he had just earned to pay the government silver in another's stead, and so preserved a whole husband and wife; and like the elder Zhang of Handan, who gave ten years' accumulated money to complete the ransom silver of another, and so kept a man's wife and children alive. These are all what is called being able to give at the place which is hard to give.

Like the elder Jin of Zhenjiang, who, old and without a son, could not bear to take a young girl as concubine and returned her to the neighbor — this is being able to forbear at the place which is hard to forbear.

Thus Heaven sends down on them abundant blessing. Those who have wealth and power find it easy to establish virtue; easy yet not doing it is self-abandonment. The poor and humble find all works of good difficult; difficult yet being able to do it is worthy of praise.

blocks.text: 3. The Ten Principles of Practicing Goodness

inline.s: To help the crowd in accord with conditions: the kinds are extremely many. To state the principles in brief, there are about ten: First, to do good together with others; second, to keep loving and reverential thoughts; third, to complete the good of others; fourth, to encourage others to do good; fifth, to rescue people in peril; sixth, to establish great benefits; seventh, to part with wealth to make blessing; eighth, to support the true Dharma; ninth, to revere and honor elders; tenth, to cherish the lives of creatures.
What is meant by doing good together with others?

In former days Shun was at Leize, and saw the fishermen all take the deep pools and the rich waters, while the old and weak fished in the swift shallows. He grieved in pity for them, and went himself to fish. When he saw those who squabbled, he concealed their faults and said nothing of them; when he saw those who yielded, he praised and held them up as a model. Within a year, they were all yielding the deep pools and rich waters to one another. Now Shun, so wise and discerning — how could he not have spoken one word to instruct the crowd? Yet he would not teach by words but turned them by his own example. This is the painstaking heart of a skilled craftsman!

We of this late age should not use our own strength to overwhelm others, nor use our own virtue to put others to shame, nor use our own many abilities to embarrass them. Gather up talent and wisdom, as though empty, as though void. When we see the faults of others, contain and cover them: on the one hand to make them able to mend, on the other to give them cause for reserve and so keep them from indulgence. When we see in others the smallest thing worth taking, or the least good worth recording, we should suddenly set aside ourselves and follow it, and moreover praise it gladly and speak of it widely. In all the uses of daily life, in saying a word and doing a thing, let us not stir a thought for ourselves but wholly set a rule for beings. This is the measure of the great man who holds the world in common.
What is meant by keeping loving and reverential thoughts?

The gentleman and the petty man, if we look merely at their outward traces, are easily confused; but at the single point of the heart's keeping, good and evil hang utterly apart, as clearly as black and white are opposite. Therefore it is said, “What makes the gentleman differ from others is the keeping of his heart.” The heart the gentleman keeps is simply a heart of loving others and revering others. For though people have near and far, noble and base, wise and foolish, worthy and unworthy — the ten thousand kinds of the unequal — all are our brothers, all are one body with us; who among them is not to be loved and revered? To love and revere the multitude is to love and revere the sages and worthies; to be able to penetrate the aims of the multitude is to penetrate the aims of the sages and worthies. Why? The aim of the sages and worthies is simply that this age and its people should each attain their proper place. If we unite love and reverence and so bring peace to the people of one age, that is to bring them peace on behalf of the sages and worthies.
What is meant by completing the good of others?

A gem in the stone is but a pebble when thrown away, but a baton of jade when polished; so whenever one sees another do a good deed, or sees that his resolve is worthy of admiration and his material can advance, one should draw him on and assist him to bring it to completion. Either reward and encourage him, or maintain and sustain him, or clear him of slander and share his blame — one must strive until he is established before stopping. Generally people hate those who are not of their own kind; in a village the good are few and the not-good many, and a good man in the vulgar world has difficulty standing on his own. And the heroic and upright, not much attending to their outward forms, are often easy to take exception to. Thus good deeds are easily spoilt and good men often get slandered; only the humane and the elder can correct and support them and help them on — their merit is the greatest.
What is meant by encouraging others to do good?

Born as human beings, who has no good conscience? The road of the world is busily toiling, and one is most easily drowned in it. Whenever one associates with others, one should conveniently rouse them and open their bewilderment. It is like one in a long night's great dream, and you make him wake once; it is like one long sunk in affliction, and you pull him into the cool. It is the most widespread kindness. Han Yu said, “To exhort one age, one uses the tongue; to exhort a hundred ages, one uses books.” Compared to doing good together with others, although this has outward form, still when the medicine suits the ailment there is often a wondrous effect, and it cannot be abandoned. When one speaks wrongly or lets a man wrongly go, one should turn and reflect upon one's own wisdom.
What is meant by rescuing people in peril?

Disaster and distress, falling and tossing, happen to everyone now and then; when one meets with them, one should take them as though a sore were upon one's own body, and quickly set about rescuing them. Either by a single word relieve their oppression, or by many means relieve their distress. Master Cui said, “The benefit need not be great; to go to the aid of a man's emergency is enough.” These are indeed the words of a humane man!
What is meant by establishing great benefits?

Small, as within one village; great, as within one whole county — whatever is beneficial, it is best to establish it. Either open a channel to direct the water, or build a dike to guard against disaster, or repair bridges to ease the traveler, or give tea and rice to relieve the hungry and thirsty. Following the occasion, exhort and guide, join strength to bring it to completion. Do not avoid suspicion; do not decline toil and reproach.
What is meant by parting with wealth to make blessing?

The myriad practices of the Buddha's gate take giving as the foremost. What is called giving is but the single word “to part with.” He who understands, within gives up the six faculties and without gives up the six sense-objects, and all that he possesses, all is given up. If one cannot yet do this, begin first by giving in wealth and material things. The world holds food and clothing as its very life, so wealth is held as the most important. We then part with it: within, to break our own stinginess; without, to relieve the urgency of others. At first it is forced, in the end it becomes calm. Nothing better washes away private feelings and removes clinging avarice.
What is meant by supporting the true Dharma?

The Dharma is the eyes of living beings in all ages. Without the true Dharma, how could one take part in Heaven and Earth? How could one fashion and finish all things? How could one escape the dust and be free of bondage? How could one pass through the world and go beyond it? Therefore whenever one sees the shrines of sages and worthies, or the scriptures and writings of the canon, one should revere and repair them. As for so raising up the true Dharma as to repay the Buddha's kindness in the highest, one should especially strive.
What is meant by revering and honoring elders?

The father and elder brothers of the home, the ruler and ministers of the state, and all who are high in years, high in virtue, high in position, or high in wisdom, should be served with particular care. At home in serving one's parents, let one keep a deep love and a gentle countenance, a soft voice and a lowly tone, until it becomes second nature; this is the root of a harmonious spirit that moves Heaven. Abroad in serving one's ruler, when one does a thing, do not think the ruler does not know and so give oneself license; when one punishes a man, do not think the ruler does not know and so exercise one's power. “Serve the ruler as Heaven” — this is an ancient maxim, and in these places the hidden virtue is most concerned. Look at families of loyalty and filial piety: their descendants are never not long-enduring and prosperous. One must indeed be heedful.
What is meant by cherishing the lives of creatures?

What makes a man truly a man is nothing but this heart of compassion. He who seeks humanity seeks this; he who accumulates virtue accumulates this. The Rites of Zhou say, “In the first month of spring, in the sacrifices, do not use a female animal”; and Mencius says, “The gentleman keeps far from the kitchen” — all to preserve this heart of compassion. Hence the ancients had the precept of the four not-eatings: not to eat what is slaughtered in one's hearing, not to eat what is slaughtered in one's sight, not to eat what is raised by oneself, and not to eat what is slaughtered specially for oneself.

Learners who cannot yet give up meat should start by abstaining in this way. Advancing gradually, the heart of compassion grows ever more; not only should killing be forbidden, but the crawling and the conscious, the moving — all are lives. To seek silk one boils the cocoon; to till the ground one kills the insects; thinking of the origin of clothing and food, one has killed them to keep oneself alive — therefore the karma of wanton waste is to be ranked with killing. As for what one strikes by hand in error, or tramples by foot in error, one knows not how many there are; one should in every way guard against them. An old poem says, “In love of the rat one always saves some food; in pity of the moth one does not light the lamp.” How humane!
Good deeds are endless and cannot be told out fully; but from these ten matters, by extending them in each direction, all the myriad virtues may be made complete!

blocks.text: Part Four. The Efficacy of the Virtue of Humility

inline.s: The Book of Changes says, “The way of Heaven diminishes the full and increases the humble; the way of Earth overturns the full and causes the humble to overflow; gods and spirits harm the full and bless the humble; the way of man hates the full and loves the humble.” Therefore in the hexagram of Humility all six lines are auspicious. The Book of History says, “Fullness invites loss; humility receives benefit.”

I have repeatedly sat the examinations together with the gentlemen, and whenever I saw a poor scholar about to succeed, there was always a certain humble radiance about him that one could scoop up in one's hands.
In the year Xinwei (

years of age) I set out for the examinations. Of my fellow students from Jiashan there were altogether ten, and only Ding Bin (courtesy name Jingyu) was the youngest, and he was extremely humble. I told Fei Jinpo, “This brother will surely pass this year.” Fei said, “How do you know?” I said, “Only the humble receive blessing. Look among the ten men — is there one modest and considerate, not daring to take precedence over others, like Jingyu? Is there one respectful and compliant, careful and reverent, like Jingyu? Is there one who, when insulted, does not answer, and when slandered, does not dispute, like Jingyu? If a man can be like this, even Heaven, Earth, gods and spirits will protect him; how could he fail to succeed?” When the roll was opened, Ding indeed passed.
In the year Dingchou (

years of age), being in the capital, I lived with Feng Kaizhi, and saw that he emptied himself and restrained his countenance, having greatly changed the habits of his youth. Li Jiyan, an upright and honest friend, often openly attacked his faults, but one only saw him accept them with an even mind, never answering a word. I told him, “Blessing has its beginning and calamity has its prelude. If this heart is truly humble, Heaven will surely assist you; this year, brother, you will certainly pass.” And so it was.

Zhao Yufeng (Guangyuan), a man of Guanxian in Shandong, was chosen at the provincial examination while still a boy, yet for a long time could not pass the higher examination. His father was the third assistant magistrate of Jiashan, and Zhao followed him to his post. He admired Qian Mingwu and took his essay to show him. Mingwu blotted out his essay entirely; Zhao was not only not angry, but was convinced at heart and quickly changed it. The next year he passed.
In the year Renchen (

years of age), I came to the court for audience and met Xia Jiansuo. I saw that his spirit was humble and his attitude lowly, and his modest radiance pressed upon one. Returning home I told a friend, “Whenever Heaven is about to raise a man, before it brightens his blessing it first brightens his wisdom; and once this wisdom breaks forth, the shallow become solid and the rampant become restrained. Jiansuo is so gentle and good — Heaven has opened the way for him.” When the roll was opened, he indeed passed.
In the year Jiawu (

years of age, Master Liaofan), at the Nanjing provincial examination, I lodged in a temple.
