When the results were announced and my name was absent, I cursed the examiners vociferously as having blinded eyes. A Daoist sat by at that time, smiling. Zhang at once turned his anger upon the Daoist. The Daoist said, “Sir, your essay must not have been good.” Zhang grew angrier, saying, “You have not seen my essay; how do you know it is not good?” The Daoist said, “I have heard that in writing an essay the heart and spirit should be peaceful and even. Now to hear you curse and rail, your heart is greatly disturbed; how can the essay be skillful?” Zhang could not but yield, and drew near to ask his instruction.

The Daoist said, “Passing depends entirely on destiny; if destiny does not ordain it, though the essay be skillful, it avails nothing. You must make a change in yourself.” Zhang said, “If it is destiny, how can one change it?” The Daoist said, “He who makes destiny is Heaven; he who establishes destiny is myself. Strive to do good deeds and broadly accumulate hidden virtue — what blessing can one not seek?” Zhang said, “I am a poor scholar; what can I do?” The Daoist said, “Good deeds and hidden merit are both made by the heart. Keep this heart constantly, and the merit is without measure. Take this matter of humility, for instance: it costs no money; why do you not turn and reflect on yourself instead of cursing the examiners?”
In the year Dingyou (

years of age, Master Liaofan), I dreamed I came to a lofty building and got a register of the examinations, in which there were many blank lines. I asked a bystander, who said, “This is the register of the present examination.” I asked, “Why are so many names missing?” He said, “In the underworld the examinations are reviewed once every three years; only one who has accumulated virtue without fault has his name listed. Those here omitted were all destined to pass, but have been struck off for new faults.” Then he pointed to a line and said, “For these three years you have held yourself with great care; perhaps you should fill this place. Take care of yourself.” That year I indeed passed, in the hundred and fifth place.

From this it can be seen that three feet above one's head there surely are spirits and gods; and that to move toward good fortune and avoid calamity is entirely up to oneself. One must keep one's heart and govern one's conduct so as not to offend in the least Heaven, Earth, gods, or spirits; and be empty of self and humble, so that Heaven, Earth, gods and spirits always pity me — only then is there the foundation of receiving blessing. Those full of pride are surely not vessels of far reach; though they rise, they have no enjoyment. A man of the smallest insight will surely not bear to narrow his own measure and so reject his own blessing. Moreover, the humble have a place to receive teaching and to take in goodness without limit, and this above all is indispensable to one who cultivates his work.

An old saying goes, “He who sets his mind upon rank and fame will surely attain rank and fame; he who sets his mind upon wealth and honor will surely attain wealth and honor.” A man's having a resolve is like a tree's having a root. Once this resolve is established, one must be humble in thought after thought and kind in matter after matter, and naturally Heaven and Earth will be moved, and the making of blessing shall rest with me.

Those who today seek to pass the examinations: at first they did not truly have a resolve; it was but a moment's excitement of mind. When the excitement comes they seek; when the excitement flags they stop. Mencius said, “If the king's delight in music were great, how near would the state of Qi be to a good state!” So it is with me also regarding rank and examination success.

blocks.text: Part One. The Study of Establishing Destiny

inline.s: In my childhood I lost my father, and my old mother ordered me to give up my studies and take up medicine. She said, “To study medicine can maintain the household and can save people; and if you can become expert in the art and be famous in the world, that is also the lifelong wish of your father.”

Later, at Ciyun Temple, I met an old man with a long beard and an extraordinary countenance, who seemed almost to float like an immortal. I bowed to him respectfully. The old man said to me, “You are by destiny a man of official life; next year you will pass the xiucai examination. Why do you not study?” I told him my reason for not studying, and asked his surname and where he lived. The old man said, “My surname is Kong, and I am from Yunnan. I received the orthodox transmission of the Imperial Ultimate numbers from Master Shao Yong of the Song dynasty. Above, I know whether a nation will flourish or decline; below, I know each person's good fortune and misfortune. By the fixed number, I am to transmit the Imperial Ultimate numbers to you.” Thereupon I invited him to my home and reported the matter to my mother, who said, “Treat him well.”

We tested Mr. Kong's Imperial Ultimate numbers, and everything he calculated, down to the finest detail, proved accurate one by one. This showed that Mr. Kong foresaw things as if by divine insight, and since he said I would pass the xiucai examination next year and afterward enter official life, I conceived the wish to study. I went to discuss it with my elder cousin Shen Cheng, who said, “Mr. Yu Haigu has opened a school at the home of Shen Youfu; it would be very convenient for me to send you there as a boarding student.” So I took Mr. Yu as my teacher.

Mr. Kong used the Imperial Ultimate numbers to calculate my prospects in the xiucai examination of the following year. He said that, sitting the county examination as a tongsheng, I would place fourteenth; in the prefectural examination, seventy-first; and in the provincial examination, ninth. When I went to the examinations the next year, the placings in all three were exactly as he had calculated, and so I passed and became a xiucai.

Mr. Kong also calculated the good and ill fortune of my whole life. He said, “In such a year you will place such a rank in the examinations; in such a year you will receive the government stipend; in such a year you will become a tribute student. In a certain year after that you will be selected to serve as county magistrate in Sichuan, and after three and a half years in office you ought to resign and return home. On the fourteenth day of the eighth month of your fifty-third year, at the hour of the ox, you will die in your own bedroom — and alas, you will have no son.” I wrote down Mr. Kong's words one by one and carefully stored them in my mind.

From then on, the placings in every examination and the order of every promotion were exactly as Mr. Kong had calculated. In one thing only did he differ: he reckoned that I would become a tribute student when my stipendiary rice reached ninety-one dan and five dou; yet when my rice had reached only a little over seventy dan, Commissioner Tu, the education commissioner, approved my promotion to tribute status. I privately wondered whether it would go through, and in the end the county's petition was indeed rejected by Mr. Yang, the acting commissioner who succeeded him.

It was not until the year dingmao that Commissioner Yin Qiuming, the education commissioner, saw the examination papers I had drafted and sighed, saying, “These five policy essays are like five memorials submitted by a great minister to the throne. How can we let a scholar of such deep and thorough learning be buried in obscurity all his life!” He therefore approved my promotion to tribute student in accordance with the county's earlier petition; and when the stipendiary rice I had eaten was reckoned together, it came to exactly ninety-one dan and five dou.

I therefore became all the more convinced that advancement and obscurity are appointed by fate, and that whether things come early or late has its fixed time. And so my heart grew cold and I sought nothing more.
After becoming a tribute student I went to Beijing, and during the year I spent there I sat in quiet meditation all day long, reading neither essays nor books.

In the year jisi I returned to Jiangnan and went to study at the Imperial Academy in Nanjing. Before enrolling, I first went to call on Chan Master Yungu and met him at Qixia Temple in the Sheshan hills. The two of us sat facing each other in a single room, and for three days and three nights I did not once doze off or fall asleep. Chan Master Yungu asked, “The reason a person cannot become a sage is only that deluded thoughts entangle him. Yet you have sat for three days and three nights without giving rise to a single deluded thought. How is this possible?”

I replied, “My fate has already been settled by Mr. Kong. Honor and disgrace, death and life, all have their fixed number. Even if I wished to have deluded thoughts, there would be nothing to think about.”

Chan Master Yungu laughed and said, “When I saw you sitting in stillness for three days and three nights with your eyes unclosed and not a deluded thought arising, I took you for someone quite extraordinary. It turns out you are only an ordinary man.”

I asked him why he called me an ordinary man. Chan Master Yungu said, “Ordinary people cannot yet reach the state of no-mind; they are forever seizing upon outer conditions and turning things over in their thoughts, and so in the end they are bound by yin and yang and inevitably have a fixed fate. But it is only the fate of ordinary people that is fixed. One of the utmost goodness, by doing deeds of the utmost goodness, turns his destiny for the better, and so the fixed number cannot hold him. One of the utmost wickedness, by doing deeds of the utmost wickedness, turns his destiny for the worse, and so the fixed number cannot hold him either. For these twenty years you have been wholly calculated by Mr. Kong, and you have not moved your fate by so much as a hair. If you are not an ordinary man, what are you?”
I asked, “Then can this fixed fate be escaped?”

Chan Master Yungu said, “‘Fate is made by oneself; blessing is sought by oneself.’ The truth set forth in the Book of Songs and the Book of History is indeed an excellent teaching. Our Buddhist scriptures say, ‘Seek wealth and honor, and you obtain wealth and honor; seek sons and daughters, and you obtain sons and daughters; seek long life, and you obtain long life.’ This is absolutely true. For the prohibition of false speech is the gravest and most essential precept in Buddhism; how could the Buddhas and bodhisattvas deceive people with false words?”

I went on to ask, “Mencius said, ‘Seek, and you will obtain it, because what is sought lies within myself.’ Virtue and benevolence rest with oneself, and I can obtain them if I strive. But rank, fame, wealth, and honor do not rest with me; if others do not grant them, how can I obtain them?”

Chan Master Yungu said, “Mencius spoke truly; it is you who have understood him wrongly. Have you not seen how the Sixth Patriarch Huineng says in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, ‘All fields of blessing are within each person's own mind; seek within your own mind, and where sincerity reaches, you will surely obtain’? To seek within oneself means to cut off evil and accumulate goodness. Then one gains virtue and benevolence within, and rank, fame, wealth, and honor without — gaining both within and without, and such seeking is effective. But if one does not reflect on one's own faults and does not strive to cut off evil and accumulate goodness, but merely gallops outward in pursuit, then even with schemes and stratagems, whether one obtains anything is wholly decided by fate. The usual result is that one gains no virtue or benevolence within and no rank or wealth without, losing both within and without: such seeking is of no use.”

Seeing that I still did not quite understand, Chan Master Yungu, prescribing the remedy to fit the illness, turned the conversation and asked me, “What exactly did Mr. Kong calculate your life would be?” I told him truthfully. Chan Master Yungu said, “Weigh it for yourself: do you deserve to pass the examinations and take office? Do you deserve to have a son?”

I reflected for a long while before answering, “I do not. Those who pass the examinations and take office mostly have the countenance of good fortune. I was born with scant blessing, and I cannot sustain a good mind and diligently do good deeds to thicken it. Moreover, I have no patience for troublesome matters, my measure is narrow, I am forever overshadowing others with my cleverness, and I indulge my temper and speak lightly and wildly. All of these are marks of scant blessing — how could I pass the examinations and take office! Filthy ground breeds living things, while clear water often holds no swimming fish; I was excessively fastidious about my own purity, to the point of being cold and inhuman — this is the first reason I ought to have no son. Harmony can give life to all things, yet I am fond of losing my temper — this is the second reason I ought to have no son. Benevolence is the root of unending life, while a cruel and unkind heart is the cause of barrenness; I cared only for guarding my own name and honor and could seldom give up myself to save others — this is the third reason I ought to have no son. Much talk drains the vital breath — this is the fourth reason I ought to have no son. Fondness for drink scatters the spirit — this is the fifth reason I ought to have no son. I often sat through the whole night in meditation without knowing how to conserve my primal vitality and nourish my spirit — this is the sixth reason I ought to have no son. As for my other faults and evils, they are still many, and I could not list them all.”

Chan Master Yungu said, “You just said, ‘Those who pass the examinations and take office mostly have the countenance of good fortune.’ In truth, it is not only rank and office: wealth and honor, and the bearing of sons, all depend on merit and virtue. Whoever in this world enjoys a fortune of a thousand pieces of gold must be a person with the reward of a thousand pieces of gold; whoever enjoys a fortune of a hundred pieces must be a person with the reward of a hundred; whoever starves to death must be a person who deserves to starve. Heaven simply carries out, exactly as it is, the fortune or misfortune each person already has — where would it add the least intention of its own? Take the matter of having sons. One who has accumulated hidden virtue for a hundred generations will surely have descendants for a hundred generations to preserve it; one who has accumulated hidden virtue for ten generations will surely have descendants for ten generations to preserve it; one who has accumulated hidden virtue for three generations or two will surely have descendants for three generations or two to preserve it. And those whose line is cut off — it is all because they have not accumulated hidden virtue!”

Now that you know where your faults lie, you must thoroughly rid yourself of the failings that have kept you from passing the examinations and from having a son. You must accumulate hidden virtue; you must be tolerant of others; you must be gentle and loving; you must cherish your spirit. Let all that belongs to the past be gone — pay it no more heed, as though you had died yesterday. Let all that belongs to the future begin anew, as though you were born today; and this reborn self of yours is a wholly new body of benevolence, righteousness, and virtue.

Even a body of flesh and blood has its fixed fate; how much more should a body of benevolence, righteousness, and virtue be able to move Heaven! The Taijia says, ‘Calamities sent down by Heaven may still be avoided; calamities you bring upon yourself you must surely suffer.’ Mr. Kong calculated that you would not pass the examinations and would not have a son: these are calamities sent down by Heaven, and they may still be escaped. Now, if you enlarge your noble character, diligently practice good deeds, and accumulate much hidden virtue, that is blessing you make for yourself — how could you fail to enjoy it?”

The Book of Changes plans for the noble man how to pursue good fortune and avoid misfortune. If the decree of Heaven were fixed and could not be changed, how could good fortune be pursued and misfortune avoided? In its very first chapter it says, ‘The family that accumulates goodness will surely have an abundance of blessings to leave to its descendants, and so its descendants will certainly flourish.’ Do you believe what I have said to you?”

Chan Master Yungu's words were like a thunderclap that wakes the deaf, and I felt as though I had woken from a dream. Believing him without a trace of doubt, I bowed respectfully and accepted his teaching. Thereupon, before the Buddha, I repented with all my heart, confessing all my past faults and evils without the least concealment; and I wrote out a petition, first seeking to pass the provincial examination, and vowed to perform three thousand good deeds to repay the grace of Heaven and Earth and of my ancestors.

Seeing that I had vowed to perform three thousand good deeds, Chan Master Yungu brought out a ledger of merit and demerit and showed it to me, telling me to record everything I did, day by day: good deeds counted as merit and entered, evil deeds counted as demerit and deducted. He also taught me to hold the mantra of Cundi, so as to guarantee that the remaking of my fate would surely succeed.

Chan Master Yungu said to me, “Those who make a profession of drawing talismans have a saying: ‘If the talisman you draw is not efficacious, even the ghosts and spirits will laugh at you.’ The secret of an efficacious talisman is this: when drawing it, do not stir a thought. When you take up the brush to draw the talisman, first set down everything in your mind, gather your attention completely, and do not let even the finest thought arise. At the moment when no thought is present, make a single dot; this dot is called the opening of the foundation of chaos, and it lays the basis for the whole talisman. From there, drawing it through in one continuous stroke without giving rise to a thought in the process, the talisman will be efficacious. Whenever one prays to Heaven or seeks to remake one's fate, one must enter the state of concentrated absorption free of stray thoughts, and thereby attain spiritual response.

To be undivided toward favorable and adverse circumstances — only then can the mind settle, only then can one be at peace in poverty and delight in the Way; this is the foundation for remaking one's fate. Confucius's disciple Yan Hui was the model of finding peace in poverty and joy in the Way. Confucius praised him, saying, ‘How worthy was Hui! A single basket of rice, a single gourd of water, dwelling in a mean lane — others could not have borne the sorrow, yet Hui did not let his joy be altered. How worthy was Hui!’

When Mencius set forth the principle of remaking one's fate, he said, ‘a short life and a long life are not two.’ And yet a short life and a long life are utterly different things! But when we do not stir our minds to love and hate, to take and reject — no thinking, no deliberating — where is there any short life or long life? Spelled out in detail: only when abundance and scarcity are seen as no different can a fate of poverty be turned into a fate of wealth; only when hardship and success are seen as no different can a fate of hardship be turned into a fate of success; only when a short life and a long life are seen as no different, with life and death set outside one's concern, can a fate of early death be turned into a fate of long life. In this human world, life and death are the weightiest matter of all, and that is why Mencius spoke only of being without discrimination between a short life and a long life. In fact, being without discrimination toward all favorable and adverse circumstances — wealth and honor, poverty and lowliness, success and hardship, long life and short life — is all contained in that one phrase.

As for ‘cultivating oneself and awaiting it,’ this is the matter of accumulating hidden virtue and praying to Heaven. As for ‘cultivating,’ it means that all one's own faults and evils should be corrected and removed; as for ‘awaiting,’ it means waiting until the work of self-cultivation is deep, and then one's fate will of itself improve. One must not harbor the least inordinate hope, nor may one pursue and curry favor; if any such thing arises, it must be utterly cut off and removed. Reaching this state, one then returns to the origin and goes back to the source, revealing the original face of purity, wisdom, and great power. This is true learning!

You cannot yet reach the state of ‘no affairs in the mind, no mind in affairs,’ but you may recite the mantra of Cundi to cultivate the mind and reach a state of concentrated absorption free of stray thoughts. When reciting the mantra, do not keep count and do not let it be interrupted. When your recitation has become thoroughly familiar, then within reciting there is no reciting, and within not reciting there is reciting; when you realize and enter the state of no-thought and yet no absence of thought, the mantra you recite will be efficacious, and spiritual response will appear of itself.”

My former style name was Xuehai. That very day I changed it to Liaofan, meaning 'no longer an ordinary man,' for I had already understood the principle of establishing one's own fate and no longer wished to be an ordinary man tossed about by destiny.

From then on I was careful and circumspect all day long, and felt myself different from before. Formerly I had been careless and self-indulgent; now I was reverent and cautious, fearing only that I might do wrong. Even where no one was present, I was ever afraid of offending Heaven, Earth, and the spirits; and when I met people who hated or slandered me, I could of myself accept it calmly and peaceably without taking account of it.

The next year I went to the preliminary examination held by the Ministry of Rites. Mr. Kong had calculated that I would place third, but I unexpectedly placed first: his words had begun to fail. And in the provincial examination that autumn I passed and became a juren.

In the early days of reforming my faults and accumulating goodness, though I strove very hard, what I ought to do still came with a certain reluctance, and my mind still held stray thoughts; examining my words and deeds, I found many remaining failures. Sometimes I saw a good deed and did it, but without pressing forward courageously; sometimes when the moment came to save someone, my mind still wavered; sometimes I forced myself to do good in action while my speech was often at fault; sometimes, while sober, I could still hold myself in check, but once drunk I ran wild. Merit offset demerit, and many days passed in vain with no goodness accumulated.

From the year jisi, when I made my vow, until the year jimao — more than ten years in all — I finally completed the three thousand good deeds I had pledged. At that time I was accompanying Li Jian'an through the pass on official business and had no chance to dedicate the merit. It was only the following year, after I had returned to my home in the south, that I asked the venerable monks Xingkong, Huikong, and others to perform the dedication at the East Pagoda Chan Hall.

When the dedication was finished, I made a vow to seek a son, and pledged to perform three thousand good deeds in return. The following year my son Tianqi was born. For every good deed I did I at once noted it down in writing; your mother, who could not write, would mark each good deed she did with a red circle stamped on the calendar with a goose quill — whether giving food to the poor or buying living creatures to set free — sometimes as many as a dozen circles in a single day. Three years passed, and by the eighth month of the year guiwei all three thousand good deeds I had pledged were completed. So I again asked the venerable Xingkong and the others to perform the dedication in our courtyard at home.

On the thirteenth day of the ninth month of that year I made a further vow to pass the jinshi examination, pledging to perform ten thousand good deeds in return. Three years later, at the age of fifty-one, I passed the jinshi examination and was appointed by the Ministry of Personnel as magistrate of Baodi County. I prepared a small ruled notebook and named it 'The Compilation of Mind-Cultivation.' Each morning, before going to the hall to attend to business, I had a servant take this notebook to the gatekeeper and set it on my desk, so that whatever good or evil I did that day, however trifling, was recorded one by one. In the evening I set a table in the courtyard, put on my official robes, lit incense, and, following the example of Zhao Yuedao, reported to the Lord of Heaven each thing I had done during the day.

Your mother, seeing that we had not done many good deeds, would knit her brows and say, “When we lived at home I helped you do good deeds, and so you were able to complete the three thousand you had pledged. Now you have pledged ten thousand good deeds, and here we live in the deep inner quarters of the magistrate's residence with nothing good to do — when will they ever be finished?” That very night I happened to see a divine being in a dream, and I told him why the ten thousand good deeds were so hard to complete. The divine being said, “By the single matter of reducing the grain levy, the ten thousand good deeds you pledged are already accomplished.”

It turned out that the grain levy in Baodi County was two fen, three li, and seven hao per mu of land. Seeing that the burden on the people was too heavy and their lives unbearably hard, I investigated the actual circumstances, reported to my superiors, and memorialized the court, and in the end the levy was reduced to one fen, four li, and six hao; so the reduction of the grain levy did indeed take place. What astonished me considerably was that the divine being knew of it and said it could count for ten thousand good deeds; whether it could truly count for so much, I was somewhat in doubt.

It happened that Chan Master Huanyu came from Mount Wutai, so I told him of the dream and asked whether it could be believed. Chan Master Huanyu replied, “If the good heart is true and earnest, then a single good deed can count for ten thousand good deeds — how much more so this reduction of the grain levy for the whole county, a great matter that brought blessing to thousands and tens of thousands of people!” Hearing his words, I became certain that I had fulfilled my vow of ten thousand good deeds, and at once donated my salary silver, asking him to feed ten thousand monks at Mount Wutai and perform the dedication for me.
Mr. Kong had calculated that I would die at fifty-three. Though I never prayed for long life, that year passed for me in peace and safety, and this year I am already sixty-nine.

The Book of History says, 'Heaven is hard to trust; the mandate is not constant.' It also says, 'The mandate is not fixed.' These words are all true and not false. From this I know that whoever says blessing and calamity are brought about by oneself speaks the words of sages and worthies, while whoever says blessing and calamity are bestowed by Heaven speaks the common talk of the world.

Your fate — who knows how it will turn out. Even if your destiny is to be honored and exalted, you should always think of decline and neglect; even if your times run smoothly, you should always think of adversity; even if you are prosperous before your eyes, you should always think of poverty; even if people love and respect you, you should be careful and circumspect and always think with fear; even if your family is of high repute, you should always think of yourself as lowly; even if your learning is rather superior, you should always think of it as shallow and meager.

Thinking far ahead, you should spread abroad the grace and virtue of your ancestors; thinking close at hand, you should make up for your parents' faults and errors with good deeds. Looking upward, think of repaying your country's grace; looking downward, think of creating blessings for your family. Outwardly, think of relieving the urgent distress of others; inwardly, think of guarding against your own evil thoughts.

You must know your own faults every day and correct your own faults every day. If for one day you do not know your faults, then for that day you rest content in the belief that you have none; if for one day you have no fault to correct, then for that day you make no progress. There are truly many clever and gifted people in the world; the reason their virtue does not grow better with cultivation and their undertakings do not grow greater is nothing but those four words, 'muddling along for present comfort,' which fritter away a whole lifetime.

The teaching on establishing one's own fate that Chan Master Yungu transmitted is the most refined, the most profound, the most true, and the most upright of principles. You must study it closely and read it again and again, come to realize its meaning for yourself, and then carry it out with all your heart and strength. Above all, do not let these fine years pass in vain!

blocks.text: Part Two. The Method of Reforming Faults

inline.s: Many of the great officers of the Spring and Autumn period could foretell a person's fortune or misfortune from his speech and bearing, and they were never wrong, as may be seen throughout the Zuo Commentary, the Guoyu, and other such records. The omens of good and ill fortune for the most part sprout in the mind and then pervade the whole body, so that they show in a person's speech and bearing. Those whose speech and bearing are steady and generous often obtain blessing; those whose speech and bearing are frivolous and mean often meet with calamity. Yet worldly people, blind as though their eyes were open, cannot see it, and so they say that fortune and misfortune are uncertain and cannot be foretold. Those great officers, however, by virtue of their utmost sincerity, were in accord with the mind of Heaven and so could perceive these omens. When they saw good omens, they knew beforehand that the person would obtain blessing; when they saw bad omens, they knew beforehand that he would meet with calamity.

blocks.text: 1. The Three Minds of Reforming Faults

inline.s: Faults and evils are the root of ruined blessing and coming calamity. Now, if one wishes to obtain blessing and keep misfortune at a distance, then before speaking of doing good and creating blessing, one must first speak of how to reform one's faults. But to reform one's faults, one must do the following:

First, one must arouse the mind of shame. Consider: the sages and worthies from ancient times and I are all alike great men. Why is it that after a hundred generations people still learn from them, while my whole life is like a roof tile shattered on the ground, worth nothing at all?

To wallow in the passions and desires of this dusty world, secretly doing all manner of things one ought not to do, and still to think that others do not know, proud and unashamed — thus day by day to sink toward the level of beasts without knowing it oneself: among the things in this world that are shameful, none is greater than this! Mencius said, 'The greatest and most essential thing for a person is to know shame.' For if one knows shame, one will strive to reform one's faults, one's virtue will be renewed day by day, and by persisting one may become a worthy or a sage. If one does not know shame, one will give free rein to one's will, gradually lose one's human character, and sink to the level of beasts. Therefore knowing shame is the key to reforming faults.

Second, one must arouse the mind of awe. Heaven and Earth are above us, and ghosts and spirits are hard to deceive; though others may not see my faults and evils, Heaven, Earth, and the spirits see them perfectly clearly.

Nor is that all. Even in a private room or a dark corner, everything I do is watched by the eyes of the spirits and pointed at by their fingers, as though in the broad light of day. However secretly I conceal it and however cleverly I gloss it over, the desire in my heart has long since shown itself, and in the end it is hard to deceive either myself or others; once someone sees through me, I am not worth a penny! How can one fail to keep a mind of reverence always present?

Nor is that all. So long as a person still has a breath left, even the greatest of crimes may still be repented and reformed. There was once a man who did evil all his life, yet repented as he lay dying, and by the arising of a single good thought he met a good end — because that single thought was utterly sincere and piercingly earnest, and so it could wash away the evil of a lifetime. It is like a deep valley dark for a thousand years: let a single lamp shine into it, and the darkness of a thousand years is wholly dispelled. Therefore, whether a fault is long-standing or newly committed, it is most precious once it is reformed.

But the affairs of this dusty world are hard to foresee, and this body of flesh is easily lost; when the breath does not return, even if one wishes to reform one's faults, there is no way left to do so. Having failed to reform them in time, one dies, and in this world of the living one bears a bad name for a thousand or a hundred years; even filial sons and compassionate grandsons cannot wash it away for him. In the world below, for a thousand or a hundred kalpas he sinks into the hells and suffers retribution; even sages, worthies, Buddhas, and bodhisattvas cannot rescue him. How can one fail to be afraid?

Third, one must arouse the mind of courage. The reason people do not reform their faults is mostly that they delay and shrink back. I must rouse myself with determination, without hesitation and without waiting. A small fault is like a fine thorn in the flesh — hard to bear, hard to endure — and one draws it out at once. A great fault is like a poisonous snake biting one's finger: to preserve one's life, one cuts off the finger at once, unafraid of the pain. There must be not the slightest hesitation or lingering; this is why swift and resolute action is so very effective.

Once one possesses the mind of shame, the mind of awe, and the mind of courage, one can reform a fault as soon as it arises. When faults and evils meet these three minds, they are like thin ice in spring meeting the sun: is there any fear that they will not melt away?

blocks.text: 2. The Three Methods of Reforming Faults

inline.s: Now, a person's faults and evils may be reformed at the level of the deed, at the level of principle, or at the level of the mind; because the methods differ, their results differ as well.

For example, if one formerly killed living beings, one now forbids oneself to kill; if one formerly lost one's temper and scolded others, one now forbids oneself to be angry: this is reforming at the level of the deed. To reform at the level of the deed is to force oneself from the outside not to transgress; it is a hundred times harder than reforming from within, and moreover the root of the disease remains. When it is stamped out in the east, it springs up in the west: this is not a way to uproot faults and evils completely.

One who is skilled at reforming faults will always make the principle clear before forbidding himself a thing. For example, if the fault lies in killing living beings, then reflect: the Lord on High delights in life and hates slaughter, and all animals love their own lives and wish to live. How can the heart be at peace when one kills them to feed oneself? Moreover, when they are killed they suffer the butcher's knife and are plunged into boiling pots and oil cauldrons, every kind of pain piercing to the marrow; while for oneself, even if the table is spread with every delicacy and the rarest seafood, once it has passed the throat no flavor can be distinguished at all. Plain vegetables and soup can fully satisfy hunger — why must one kill them and so diminish one's own share of blessing?

Reflect further: creatures with flesh and blood and breath all have a spirit and awareness; since they have a spirit and awareness, they are one of us. Even if I cannot cultivate such lofty virtue as to make them respect me and draw near to me, how can I kill them day after day and make them hate and resent me without end? As soon as this thought arises, one will grieve over such food and be unable to eat it.

For example, if one is given to anger, one must reflect: if another's ability falls short and a matter is not handled well, by all reason I ought to pity him. If he offends me unreasonably, the fault is his — why should I flare up and torment myself? Therefore there is truly nothing to be angry about.

Reflect further: in all the world there is no such thing as a hero who thinks himself always right, nor such a thing as learning that lays the blame on others. When a matter fails, it is always because one's own virtue is not well cultivated and cannot move others to support me and join me in finishing it with one heart.

Whenever I meet with anything contrary, I look for the cause entirely in myself. In this way, all slander becomes a fine opportunity to temper me, raise me up, and bring me to accomplishment; I have not even time to be grateful — how could I be angry?

Moreover, if others slander and attack me, so long as I do not grow angry, then however fierce their bluster, it is no more than raising a torch to burn the empty sky, where there is nothing to burn, and the fire goes out of itself. But if I grow angry when slandered and attacked, then even if I strain my wits to argue cleverly, I am only spinning a cocoon that binds me, bringing on endless entanglement; thus anger is not only useless but harmful.
As for the many other kinds of faults and evils, all should be considered according to principle. Once the principle is clear, the fault will no longer be committed.

What does it mean to reform at the level of the mind? Though faults and evils number thousands and tens of thousands, all are made by the mind. If my mind is not seduced by things, objects, passions, and circumstances into giving rise to bad thoughts, where can faults and evils arise? One who cultivates virtue need not seek out the many faults — lust for beauty, lust for fame, lust for wealth, lust for anger — and reform them one by one by principle or by deed; so long as the right thought of single-minded goodness is present before him, deviant thoughts cannot of themselves defile him. It is like the sun standing in the sky: goblins and spirits all flee into hiding. This is the true transmission of the one that governs the ten thousand! Faults are made by the mind, and so they must also be reformed by the mind, like cutting down a poisonous tree by severing its root directly — why hack at it branch by branch and strip it leaf by leaf?

In sum, the highest method of reforming faults is governing the mind, keeping the mind pure and calm at all times and in all places. Because the mind is pure, as soon as a bad thought stirs it is like a stain on snow-white cloth — one becomes aware of it at once, and the moment one is aware, one clears it away. With no bad thoughts, there will naturally be no bad words or deeds. If one's skill in governing the mind is insufficient, and one cannot yet reach the point where an evil thought 'is noticed the moment it stirs, and vanishes the moment it is noticed,' then one must take up reforming by principle, using reasoned reflection to drive out the fault, as in the examples above of killing living beings and of anger. If reforming by principle is also beyond one, then one must take up reforming by deed, forbidding the deed at once whenever a fault is about to be committed. To practice reforming by mind, which is the higher skill, while also practicing reforming by principle and by deed, which are the lower, is the safest course of all. But to use only the lower skills of reforming by principle and by deed, without understanding how to apply the higher skill of reforming by mind — or even to be ignorant of reforming by principle and know only reforming by deed — is to reform one's faults without enough wisdom.

Yet when one vows to reform one's faults, one must have good friends in this world to remind one when one is confused or slack, and in the unseen realm there must be ghosts and spirits to bear witness. This is because ghosts and spirits have spiritual powers, and all that a person does and thinks is perfectly clear to them; when they attest that you have reformed your faults, then you have truly reformed them. This too is the meaning of the ancients' saying, 'Do not deceive in the dark chamber.' One must repent with a single mind, unremitting day and night; after one seven-day period, two seven-day periods, and on to one month, two months, three months, there will surely be signs of efficacy. Perhaps one feels the mind and spirit at ease and expansive; or feels wisdom suddenly opened; or, amid tangled and tumultuous affairs, suddenly finds thoughts arising that settle everything clearly and neatly; or, meeting enemies and foes, one feels not the least resentment but rather joy in the heart; or one dreams of vomiting black things; or dreams of sages and worthies of old reaching out to guide and receive one; or dreams of flying and strolling through the heavens; or dreams of Buddhas and bodhisattvas. All such excellent things are signs that faults are dissolved and offenses wiped away.

However, one must not become arrogant and self-satisfied over this, or stand still in one's tracks. In the past, Master Qu Boyu worked extremely hard at correcting his faults. At the age of twenty, he thought he had already corrected all the faults and evils of the past. By twenty-one, he realized that at twenty he had not yet finished correcting them. At twenty-two, looking back on his twenty-first year, he realized that during that period he had still been muddled, and the faults he ought to have corrected were not yet corrected. But he persisted steadfastly, year after year, each year improving upon the foundation of the previous one. Even at age fifty, he still knew that at forty-nine there were places where his correction had not been thorough. So diligent was the ancients' learning of correcting their faults! We are all in the class of ordinary people, and our many faults and evils cluster upon us like the quills of a hedgehog; yet when we look back on the past, we often see no faults at all — this is entirely due to carelessness, our eyes blinded by selfishness and desire.

However, those whose faults and evils are deep and heavy also show signs: sometimes the mind is dull and blocked, forgetting as soon as one turns one's head; sometimes one is troubled for no reason; or upon seeing a person of lofty virtue, one feels ashamed and downcast; or upon hearing proper and upright speech, one is displeased; or when one does others good, one instead draws their resentment; or one often has bad dreams, even speaks wildly, and loses the spirit of being human — all these are the appearance of having done evil. If such phenomena occur, one must certainly stir oneself to effort, and before the disaster arrives, discard the old and seek the new, cut off evil and cultivate good — by all means do not delude yourself!

blocks.text: Part Three: The Way of Accumulating Good

inline.s: The Classic of Changes says: "A household that accumulates good is sure to have an abundance of blessings left to bequeath to its descendants." In the past, when the Yan family was considering giving their daughter in marriage to Confucius' father, they recounted at length the long accumulation of virtue in his ancestors, and thereby foresaw that his descendants would surely flourish. Confucius praised Shun as a great filial son, saying: "Because of the utmost sincerity of his filial heart, when he sacrificed to his ancestors in the ancestral temple he moved them to come and receive the offering; his virtue and blessings are deep, and his descendants, generation after generation, will pass them on." These are all exceedingly accurate and profound judgments; now I will use events that have already happened in the past to verify and prove them.

Yang Rong, who rose to the rank of Junior Tutor, was a man of Jianning Prefecture, whose family for generations had made their living by ferrying a boat. Because of a torrential rain that lasted days on end, the river swelled high, the floodwaters destroyed the dwellings of the residents, and the drowned drifted downstream. The other boats were all busy salvaging the goods, but only Yang Rong's great-grandfather and grandfather were busy rescuing people, taking nothing of the drifting goods. The people of the village all mocked them as foolish.

By the time Yang Rong's father was born, the family's circumstances had gradually grown comfortable. A supernatural being, appearing in the form of a Daoist, said to Yang Rong's father: "Because your grandfather and father have hidden virtue, their descendants will become great officials, wealthy and honored. You should bury them in such-and-such a place; the feng shui there is very good." Thereupon Yang Rong's father buried his grandfather and father at the place the Daoist indicated. This tomb is now famous; it is what people call the White Rabbit Tomb.

Later Yang Rong was born. At twenty he passed the highest examination and rose in office to the Three Dukes; the emperor even conferred upon his great-grandfather, grandfather, and father the same official rank as his own. His descendants are honored and numerous, and to this day there are still many among them of virtue and ability.

Yang Zicheng of Yin County was at first a clerk in the county magistrate's office. His heart was kind and generous, and he observed the law with fairness. At that time the magistrate was very stern and severe. Once he ordered an attendant to beat a prisoner until blood flowed all over the ground, yet he was still angry without cease, and even commanded another beating. Yang Zicheng, seeing this, was deeply distressed, and knelt down to plead for mercy on the prisoner's behalf. The magistrate said, "With your intercession, I could well pardon him; but this man, having broken the law, still argues stubbornly — it is impossible not to be angered." Yang Zicheng kowtowed and said, "The corruption and tyranny of those in office, and the scattering of the people's hearts, has lasted long. When a case is examined and the truth is obtained, one ought to grieve for those involved and pity them — by no means rejoice and be pleased, lest one misjudge. If one must not even rejoice, how much less should one be angry? For under anger, it is very easy to extort a confession by torture!" Hearing Yang Zicheng's words, the magistrate was deeply moved and so let his anger subside.

Yang Zicheng's family was extremely poor. Because the position in the yamen carried a good deal of power, many people came to give gifts, but he refused them all. Whenever prisoners in the jail had nothing to eat, he would always find some way to relieve them. One day several new prisoners arrived with nothing to eat, and his own household was short of rice. If he gave the little rice the family had to the prisoners, then his own family would have nothing to eat; if he ate it himself, then the prisoners would be pitifully starving. So Yang Zicheng discussed it with his wife. His wife asked him, "Where do these prisoners come from?" He replied, "They come from Hangzhou. Along the way they had nothing to eat, enduring hunger to make it here, their faces all sallow." Thereupon husband and wife took out the rice they had been waiting to eat, cooked it into congee, and gave it to the prisoners.

Later two sons were born: the elder, Yang Shouchen, and the younger, Yang Shouzhi. One became Vice Minister of Personnel in Nanjing, the other Vice Minister of Personnel in Beijing. The eldest grandson rose to Vice Minister of Justice, and the second grandson became the Corruption Commissioner of Sichuan. These four men were all renowned officials. Yang Chuting and Yang Dezheng, whom we know today, are both descendants of Yang Zicheng.

In the past, during the Zhengtong era, Deng Maoqi rebelled in Fujian, and many scholars and common people followed him. The court appointed Zhang Kai of Yin County, who had once served as Censor-in-Chief, to lead troops south to Fujian to suppress the rebellion, and by stratagem he captured Deng Maoqi. Later Zhang Kai commissioned a Director of Affairs surnamed Xie under the Fujian Provincial Administration Commission to search out and seize the remnants in the eastern part of Fujian, ordering him to kill any he caught.

Director Xie would not slaughter the innocent indiscriminately, so he found a way to obtain the register of those who had attached themselves to Deng Maoqi. To every person not named in the register he secretly gave a small white cloth flag, and told him: on the day the government troops arrive, plant this white flag at your door. At the same time he strictly forbade the soldiers: no household that has planted a white flag may be killed arbitrarily. In this way more than ten thousand people were saved.
Later Director Xie's son, Xie Qian, took first place in the highest examinations and rose to the office of Grand Chancellor; his grandson Xie Pi also took third place.

In the Lin family of Putian County, Fujian, there was an elderly woman of the older generation who loved to do good. She often gave rice-flour dumplings to the poor. Whenever someone came asking, she would give them at once, never with a look of weariness. A transcendent being, appearing as a Daoist, came every morning to ask for six or seven dumplings. The old woman gave them to him every day, the same for three years without a hint of impatience. Thereupon the transcendent knew that her good deeds came from a heart of utmost sincerity. So he said to her, "I have eaten your dumplings for three years; how should I repay you? Behind your house there is a plot of land. If you are buried there, your descendants who become officials and are enfeoffed will be as many as the seeds in a liter of sesame." When she died, her son, following the place indicated, buried her there. In the first generation alone nine people passed the highest examinations, and afterwards many of every generation held great office — so much so that in Fujian there is a folk rhyme: "Without the Lins no list is opened; when the list is opened, the Lins are surely there."

Grand Historian Feng, whose name was Qi and whose courtesy name was Zhuo'an — in those days his father was a student at the county school. Rising early one bitterly cold winter day to go to school, he met a man lying fallen in the snow. Feeling his body, he found him already half frozen to death. So he took off his fur robe and wrapped it around him, and carried him back to his own home, where he revived him. That night he dreamed a supernatural being told him, "You saved a man's life out of a heart of utmost sincerity. I will have Han Qi be born into your family as your son." So when Grand Historian Feng was later born, he was given the name Qi.

A Minister surnamed Ying of Taizhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, studied diligently in the mountains in the prime of his life, preparing for the examinations. At night many ghosts wailed long and short, gathering all around him, most frighteningly; but he was not afraid at all.

One night he heard a ghost say, "A certain woman — because her husband has been long away and not returned, and because her parents-in-law think their son has died abroad, are forcing her to remarry. She is resolved not to consent; tomorrow night she will hang herself here. Now I have found my substitute." Lord Ying thereupon secretly sold his own fields, received four taels of silver, and, pretending to be her husband, wrote a letter and sent it with the silver to her home. At first, seeing that the handwriting did not match, the old couple were somewhat suspicious. But then they thought, "A letter can be forged, but who would forge silver? We suppose our son is safe and sound." So they no longer pressed the daughter-in-law to remarry. Later their son returned, and the couple were not separated, living well together as before.

Lord Ying again heard the ghost say, "I had already found my substitute, but this scholar ruined my great scheme." A ghost beside him said, "Then why do you not harm him?" That ghost answered, "Because this man's heart is good, the Lord on High has already decreed that he be made a Minister of Hidden Virtue. How could I harm him!"

Because of this, Lord Ying applied himself the more diligently, strictly disciplining himself; his good accumulated day by day, and his virtue deepened day by day. Whenever there was a famine year, he always contributed grain from his own household to relieve the starving. When relatives were in acute difficulty, he always thought of every means to help them through. When he met unreasonable words and deeds, he always sought the cause within himself, accepting them calmly and without dispute. His descendants who passed the examinations are many down to this day.

Xu Shi of Changshu County, Jiangsu, had the style name Fengzhu. His father had always been wealthy; whenever there was a famine year, he was always the first to remit rents, setting an example for the whole county, and he also took out a portion of his own grain to relieve the poor families.

At night he heard ghosts singing at his door: "Never false, never false — the Xu family scholar has become a provincial graduate." The calls went on ceaselessly all through the night. That year Xu Fengzhu indeed passed the provincial examination. His father therefore accumulated virtue all the more, diligently doing good without the least slack — repairing bridges and roads, feeding monks and helping the multitudes; and to every matter that could benefit people he gave his whole heart.
Later he again heard ghosts singing at his door: "Never false, never false — the Xu family graduate rises straight to the chief tribunal." Xu Fengzhu's office indeed rose to Governor of the Two Zhe.

Tu Kangxi of Jiaxing Prefecture was at first a Secretary in the Ministry of Justice. At night he lodged in the prison and questioned each prisoner condemned to death in detail about the circumstances of his case, discovering a number of the innocent. But Lord Tu did not claim the credit for himself; rather, he secretly wrote these circumstances into a memorial and reported it to the Minister of Justice. Later, when the death sentences were re-examined, the Minister of Justice used the words of the memorial to examine these prisoners — none did not submit — and because of it released over ten people who had been wrongfully accused and had confessed under torture. For a time the whole capital praised the Minister of Justice's sagacity.

Lord Tu also reported to the Minister of Justice, saying, "Beneath the feet of the Son of Heaven, in the capital itself, there are still so many wronged people; across a country this vast, with people in their tens of millions, how could there be none who are wronged? There should be, once every five years, a commission of officers to reduce sentences sent to each province to verify the cases and rectify the unjust imprisonments." The Minister of Justice presented Lord Tu's proposal to the court, and it was approved. At that time Lord Tu himself was one of the commissioned officers sent to reduce sentences.

That night he dreamed a supernatural being told him, "Your destiny has no son. Now your proposal to reduce sentences accords deeply with Heaven's mind; the Lord of Heaven grants you three sons, who in the future will all become great officials." That very night Lord Tu's wife became pregnant, and later she bore three sons: Yingxun, Yingkun, and Yingling, all of whom became eminent high officials.

Bao Ping of Jiaxing County, whose courtesy name was Xinzhi — his father was the Prefect of Chiyang Prefecture. He had seven sons, and Bao Ping was the youngest; he was taken as a son-in-law into the Yuan family of Pinghu County, and his friendship with my father was very deep, with frequent visits between them. His learning was broad and his talent overflowing, yet he took the provincial examinations several times without passing, and in ordinary times he liked to study Buddhism and Daoism.

One day he roamed east to Mao Lake, and chanced upon a temple in a village. Seeing the image of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva wet all over, he immediately opened his bag, took out ten taels of silver, and gave them to the presiding monk, asking him to repair the dilapidated and leaking halls. The monk told him, "The work is great; ten taels is too little; it cannot be completed." Bao Ping further took out four bolts of cloth produced in Songjiang, and from his bamboo trunk took out seven garments, and gave them to the monk. Among them the hemp-lined jacket had been newly made on this visit to Songjiang Prefecture, and his servant urged him to stop. Bao Ping said, "If only I can make the sacred image secure — what does it matter if I go naked and bare-bodied?" The monk was moved to tears and said, "Giving silver, cloth, and garments is not so hard; but this heart of utmost sincerity of yours — that is truly most difficult!"

Later, when the halls were repaired, Bao Ping took his father to tour them, and stayed the night in the temple. He dreamed that the Dharma-protecting spirit came to thank him, saying, "Your son will enjoy the blessing of holding office for generations." Later his son Bao Bian and his grandson Bao Chengfang both passed the highest examinations and became eminent high officials.

In Jiashan County, Zhejiang, there was a man named Zhi Li. His father, Lord Zhi, was a clerk in charge of criminal matters. A prisoner, falsely accused by others and sentenced to death, was greatly pitied by Lord Zhi, who sought a way to save him. This prisoner said to his wife, "Lord Zhi's kindness — I am ashamed that I have no way to repay it. Tomorrow invite him to the countryside; if you give yourself to serve him, perhaps he will do his utmost to exonerate me, and then I can live." His wife agreed, weeping. When Lord Zhi arrived, the prisoner's wife came out in person to offer him drink and told Lord Zhi all her husband's intention. Lord Zhi would not hear of it at all, and continued to do his utmost to clear her husband, and at last rectified this unjust case.

When this prisoner was released from prison, husband and wife came to his door to kowtow their thanks, saying, "Your great virtue like this is rare in recent ages. You have no son as yet; I wish to give you my little daughter as a concubine to sweep the floor. This is proper and in accord with ritual." Lord Zhi then prepared the betrothal gifts and formally married their daughter, and so Zhi Li was born. At twenty, Zhi Li went to take the provincial examination and passed as one of the top five — the Classic Exemplar — and later served in the Hanlin Academy in the post of secretary. Zhi Li begot Zhi Gao; Zhi Gao begot Zhi Lu, who were both selected as instructors in the prefectural and county schools. Zhi Lu's son, Zhi Dalun, passed the highest examination.

The ten examples given above, though they do different things, when summed up are all a single word: "good." If we speak more precisely, good has true and false, upright and crooked, hidden and manifested, right and wrong, partial and correct, half and full, great and small, difficult and easy — all of these should be clearly distinguished. If one does good without understanding the principle, and so thinks one has been doing good all along, one is in fact accumulating evil — wasting all one's pains to no benefit at all.

What is called true good and false good? In the past, several scholars went to pay their respects to Dhyana Master Zhongfeng. They asked, "Buddhists say that the retribution of good and evil follows one like a shadow follows its form. Now here is a certain man who is good, yet his descendants do not flourish; another man is evil, yet his family is prosperous. If so, the Buddha's words have no basis!"

Dhyana Master Zhongfeng said, "Ordinary people have not washed away their worldly feelings and lack right knowledge and right views, and so take good for evil and call evil good — this happens often. They do not repent their own inversion of right and wrong; how can they instead blame Heaven for a mistaken retribution?" The crowd said, "Good is good and evil is evil — how could they possibly be inverted?" Dhyana Master Zhongfeng then asked them to try to set forth the circumstances of doing good and doing evil. One man said, "Scolding and beating others is evil; respecting and treating others with propriety is good." Dhyana Master Zhongfeng said, "Not necessarily." Another said, "Coveting wealth and demanding money greedily is evil; being incorruptible and principled is good." Dhyana Master Zhongfeng said, "Not necessarily." The crowd then related one after another the things they had seen and heard, of "doing good and meeting calamity, doing evil and gaining blessing." Dhyana Master Zhongfeng said they were all mistaken — calling evil good and taking good for evil.

Thereupon they asked Dhyana Master Zhongfeng: just what is good and what is evil? Dhyana Master Zhongfeng told them, "To benefit others is good; to benefit oneself is evil. If it benefits others, then beating and scolding are good. If it benefits oneself, then respecting and treating others with propriety are evil. Therefore, when a person does good, what benefits others is public, and the public is true good; what benefits oneself is private, and the private is false good. Moreover, what comes forth from the heart is true good; what is done for show is false good. Doing good without any seeking is true good; doing good with some seeking is false good. All of these one should examine and distinguish carefully oneself."

What is called upright good and crooked good? Now when people see a cautious, compliant goody-goody, most call him a good person and like him. But the sage would rather choose those who are bold in advancing and untrammeled by petty formalities, considering them good persons, because they dare to act and dare to take responsibility. As for the goody-goody, though the whole village likes him, he is in truth a thief of the morals of the age and the people, because he has no principles and drifts with the current; and under his influence the morals of the age and the people are ruined without anyone being aware. This shows that the criteria of good and evil of the world are plainly the opposite of those of the sage.

Following this out, the standards of taking and rejecting of the worldly are all absurd and inverted. Yet the standard by which Heaven, Earth, ghosts, and spirits bless good and punish evil is the same as the sage's, and does not comply with the views of the world. Therefore, whoever wishes to accumulate good must by no means bend to the talk and views of the world, but must, from the depths of the mind, silently wash and purify, remove selfishness and desires, and act according to the sage's standard of good and evil.

To do good out of a pure heart of benefiting the world is upright good; if there is the slightest heart of pleasing the world, it is crooked good. To do good out of a pure heart of loving others is upright good; if there is any heart of resentment toward the world, it is crooked good. To do good out of a pure heart of respecting others is upright good; if there is any heart of trifling with the world, it is crooked good. All should be carefully distinguished.

What is called hidden good and manifest good? Whenever good is done and known to others, it is manifest good; when good is done and not known to others, it is hidden virtue. Hidden virtue, Heaven repays with blessing; manifest good enjoys the praise of the world, and praise is also a blessing.

Fame is what Heaven envies and loathes. Those in the world who enjoy a great reputation not matching their substance are mostly visited with strange calamities; those who persist in doing good despite naked slander, their descendants often suddenly flourish. Between hidden virtue and manifest good the retribution is indeed most subtle. What is called right good and wrong good? The law of the state of Lu provided that if anyone paid money to redeem the common people who had been taken captive in war by enemy states and made slaves or maidservants, restoring them to freedom, the government would, according to the regulation, give a sum of money as reward. Confucius' disciple Zigong redeemed these slaves and servants but did not accept the government's reward. Hearing this, Confucius said angrily, "Zigong is wrong! The sage in his dealings can transform customs and inculcate good, serving as a model for the multitude to teach the people, and should not seek only his own satisfaction. Now in Lu the rich are few and the poor many; Zigong's act is as if to tell the multitude that to accept the government's reward is to be greedy for wealth, and so he was unwilling to accept. In this way everyone will fear the ill name of greed — how then will anyone go to redeem people? From now on, no one will go to the nobles to redeem people."

Confucius' disciple Zilu rescued a man from the water. The man gave him an ox in gratitude, and Zilu accepted it. Confucius, hearing of it, said joyfully, "Henceforth the people of Lu who are brave in rescuing others from the water will be more and more numerous!" Because Zilu and the man who gave the ox set up a good model: the one brave in rescuing from peril, the other generous in repaying virtue. In this way a good social atmosphere will be formed.

From the worldly point of view, Zigong's not accepting the reward was good, and Zilu's accepting the ox was not good. But Confucius praised Zilu and condemned Zigong. This shows that the sage's views often differ from the world's. We should emulate the sage, and then we will accord with Heaven's mind.

Thereupon one knows: in a person's doing good, one does not look at the present moment but at whether it has harmful consequences; not at one time but at the long run; not at one person but at the whole world. What appears now to be a good deed, but when it spreads abroad is enough to harm people, is like good yet in fact not good; what appears now to be not good, but when it spreads abroad is enough to help people, is like not good yet in fact good.

However, here we have discussed only this one matter of "the good that is not good." Others, such as the righteousness that is not righteousness, the propriety that is not propriety, the trustworthiness that is not trustworthiness, the kindness that is not kindness — all should be distinguished and chosen.

What is called partial and correct? In the past, when Lord Lu Wenyi had just resigned from the post of Grand Chancellor and returned to his hometown, the whole nation regarded him with great esteem. A man of the village, drunk, came before Lord Lu's residence and cursed him loudly. Lord Lu was not angry, and said to his servant, "A drunken man — do not contend with him. Shut the gate and pay him no heed."

A year passed, and this man committed a capital crime and was imprisoned. Only then did Lord Lu regret it, saying, "If at the time I had contended with him a little, sent him to the yamen to be punished, then through this small punishment I could have greatly warned him. At the time I only thought of being kind-hearted and letting him go, not realizing I was fostering his arrogance and evil, until finally he committed a capital crime!" This is an example of doing an evil deed with a good heart.

There is also doing a good deed with an evil heart. For example, in a famine year, a great wealthy household saw the poor people robbing food in the streets in broad daylight. He reported it to the county, but the magistrate, fearing trouble, ignored it, and the poor became ever more audacious. Thereupon this wealthy household privately sent people to seize the robbers and imprison them, and expose their shame; only then did the poor settle down. Otherwise the market would have fallen into disorder.

Therefore, good is correct and evil is partial — this everyone knows. Those who do evil deeds with a good heart, like Lord Lu mentioned above, are the partial within the correct; those who do good deeds with an evil heart, like the wealthy household mentioned above, are the correct within the partial. This everyone must know.

What is called half good and full good? The Classic of Changes says, "If good is not accumulated, it is not enough to establish a name; if evil is not accumulated, it is not enough to bring the disaster of death." The Book of History says, "The evil of the Shang dynasty, accumulated one thing after another, has now filled up." Accumulating good is likewise like putting things into a container: if one puts them in diligently and constantly, it soon fills; if one is slack and does not accumulate, it will not fill. This is one account of half good and full good.

In the past, a woman came to a temple wishing to make an offering, but had not much money; she took out the two coppers she had on her and offered them. To her surprise, the abbot came in person to repent on her behalf of her karmic hindrances. Later she entered the palace, became wealthy and honored, and took several thousand taels of silver to offer at this temple, but the abbot only had his disciples turn the merit back for her. Completely bewildered, she asked, "The last time I offered only two coppers, and you repented in person for me; now I offer several thousand taels of silver, and you do not turn the merit for me. Why?" The abbot replied, "The last time, though your money was little, your heart was extremely sincere; if I had not repented in person for you, it would not have been enough to repay your merit. Now, though your money is great, your heart is not as sincere as before; I have others do the repenting on your behalf, and that suffices." Therefore, if the heart is not sincere, a thousand gold is but half good; if the heart is sincere, two coppers are full good.

Zhongli handed the elixir to Master Lü, which could turn iron into gold, to be used to save the world. Master Lü asked, "This gold is transformed from iron; in the end will it change back?" Zhongli replied, "After five hundred years it will revert to iron." Master Lü said, "To be able to turn iron to gold is indeed quite remarkable and could help many people, but it would bitterly harm the people of five hundred years hence; I am unwilling to do it." Zhongli said, "Cultivating immortality requires accumulating three thousand good deeds, but this one sentence of yours has already fulfilled those three thousand good deeds." This is another account of half good and full good.

Moreover, if one does good and does not keep the deed in the mind, then whatever good is done, great or small, is full good; if one keeps the deed in the mind, though one does it diligently all one's life, one only attains half good.

For example, when using wealth to help others, if within one does not see oneself, without one does not see the recipient, and between one does not see the wealth given — this is the emptiness of the three wheels, this is single-minded purity. Doing thus, one bushel of grain can plant boundless, measureless blessing, and one copper can wipe away the offenses of a thousand kalpas. If in the mind one still recollects that I gave wealth to such a one and I did such a good deed, then though one uses ten thousand taels of gold, it is only half good, and the blessing planted is not full. This is yet another account of half good and full good.

What is called great good and small good? In the past, when Wei Zhongda was serving in the Hanlin Academy, his soul was summoned to the underworld. The official in charge ordered the clerk to present the two records of his good and evil. When the records arrived, the evil record actually filled the whole hall, while the good record was only a small thin roll, like a single chopstick. The official ordered a scale to weigh them; the evil record filling the hall was in fact light, while that roll as thin as a chopstick was in fact heavy.

Zhongda asked, "I am not yet past forty; how can my faults and evils be so many?" The official replied, "A single thought not upright is a fault or evil; it does not wait until you actually commit it." Zhongda then asked again, "What is written in that small roll?" The official said, "Once the emperor wished to undertake a great project, building the Three Mountains stone bridge in Fujian Prefecture. You feared it would weary the people and waste money, and so you submitted a memorial to dissuade him. This is the draft of that memorial."

Zhongda said, "Though I submitted the memorial, the court did not heed it, and it did no good; how could it have such great power of good?" The official replied, "Though the court did not heed it, your single thought was already for the myriad people; had it been heeded, the power of good would be even greater." Therefore, if a good deed is for the sake of the people of the world and the state, then though the matter is small, its merit is great; if it is for the sake of a single individual, then though the matter is great, its merit is small.

What is called difficult and easy? In the past the former sages said, "To restrain one's selfish desires and control one's conduct, one must begin where it is difficult to restrain and difficult to control, and keep on restraining and controlling."

One must be like the venerable Mr. Shu of Jiangxi Province. Teaching in another place, on the road home he met a woman weeping bitterly, because her husband, in debt to the government for silver, was forced to sell his wife. He gave all the salary he had earned in two years of hard work to pay on her behalf, so that the couple were not separated. One must also be like the Elder Zhang of Handan County. He saved money in a jar, and only after ten years was it full. A neighbor had to sell his wife to pay for a crime, and his three children were still young. Elder Zhang, fearing that after she left the three children could not be raised, and that the woman could hardly live, gave all the money he had saved over ten years to pay the redemption silver on their behalf, saving the mother and her four. These are the cases of being able to give up where it is hard to give up.

Another is the Elder Jin of Zhenjiang Prefecture. At fifty, with no son, his wife sold her ornaments to buy the neighbor's daughter to be his concubine, hoping she would bear him a son. When Elder Jin returned home and discovered this, unable to bear to marry so young a woman, he immediately sent her back to the neighbor. This is being able to endure where it is hard to endure.
Because they could give up at the hard-to-give-up and endure at the hard-to-endure, so the blessings Heaven bestowed upon them were likewise very deep.

For those with wealth and power, to establish merit and virtue is everywhere very easy; to be easy and yet not do it is to waste oneself. For the poor and lowly, to do good and cultivate blessing is everywhere very hard; to be hard and yet able to do it — this is truly most precious.

Doing good is according with conditions to rescue the many, and so its kinds are extremely numerous. Summed up, there are roughly ten categories: first, being good with others; second, keeping a mind of love and respect; third, helping others perfect their good; fourth, urging others to do good; fifth, rescuing others in peril; sixth, building the great benefit; seventh, giving wealth to create blessing; eighth, upholding the true Dharma; ninth, honoring and respecting elders and superiors; tenth, cherishing the lives of beings.

What is called being good with others? In the past, Shun, by the shore of Thunder Lake, saw that the young and strong fishermen all took the deep pools and eddies rich in fish, while the old and weak could only fish at the rapids and shallows, and of course caught no fish. Shun's heart could not bear it; pitying these old and weak ones, he too went fishing. When Shun saw those who contended for the spots, he avoided speaking of their faults; when he saw those who yielded, he praised them everywhere and emulated them. After a year, everyone was yielding to one another the deep pools and confluences.

With Shun's bright and penetrating wisdom, how could he not have spoken a discourse to instruct everyone? The reason he did not use words, but through the example of his own conduct gently transformed the hearts of people and the manners of the age — this is precisely the painstaking care of a master craftsman's design!

We live in an age when customs and morals are steadily decaying, and to be a person is no easy matter. We must learn to be deeply considerate of others: do not use your own strengths to overshadow or suppress them; do not use your own cleverness to make others appear inferior; do not use your own abilities to set off the clumsiness and incompetence of others. Rather, rein in and conceal your talents, and conduct yourself in plain sincerity.

When you see another person's faults, be lenient and tolerant for the time being, and cover for him. On the one hand this gives him the chance to correct his mistakes; on the other, it keeps him from abandoning all restraint and sinking still deeper into self-indulgence. When you see that another has a small excellence worth taking up, or a modest good deed worth learning from, put aside entirely whatever in yourself falls short of him, earnestly imitate him, and ceaselessly praise him and make his good points widely known.

In ordinary times, the words one utters and the deeds one performs are not for one's own sake alone, but to set an example for the multitude. This is the vast capacity of the morally noble person, who regards the world as the possession of all alike.

What does it mean to cherish a heart of love and respect? Judged by outward appearance and conduct, the noble person and the petty person are often hard to tell apart; but in the disposition of their hearts they are utterly different. The noble person keeps a heart of goodness, the petty person a heart of evil — as different as white and black, entirely opposite.

Therefore it is said: "What distinguishes the noble person from the crowd lies in the difference of his heart alone." The heart the noble person harbors is simply a heart that loves others and respects others.

For people differ in closeness and distance, in rank and station, in wisdom and folly, in worth and worthlessness, in countless ways they are not alike; yet all are my fellow beings, one body with me. How could any one of them fail to deserve my love and reverence?
To love and revere the multitude is to love and revere the sages; to understand the wishes of the multitude is to understand the wishes of the sages.

Why is that so? Because the wish of the sages is, from the very first, that every person in this world should find his proper place. If I love and revere all people and cause each of them to find his proper place, then I am carrying out the great aspiration of the sages.

What does it mean to help others accomplish what is good?
