While jade still lies hidden in the rock and has not been cut out, if it is cast away it is worth no more than broken tiles and rubble; but once it is discovered, cut out, and polished, it becomes a precious treasure. Therefore, whenever you see a person do a good deed, or see that someone's aspiration is admirable and his natural gifts can be cultivated, you should teach and lift him up so that he may succeed. Either commend and promote him, or lend him your support, or clear away the slander and injustice he suffers and share in bearing the blame that befalls him. Do not let go until he has come to accomplishment.

Ordinarily people detest those who are not of their own kind. In any locality there are always fewer good people than bad, so that the good find it hard to gain a foothold among the worldly. Moreover, those of outstanding talent and intelligence are often upright and unbending in temperament and heedless of petty conventions, and so are all the more apt to draw blame and criticism. Thus good undertakings often fail, and good people often suffer slander. Only when humane and elder men correct these corrupting ways and lend their aid to good people in accomplishing good deeds is the greatest merit done.

What does it mean to urge others to be good? Born into this world as human beings, who among us lacks a conscience? Yet each of us, along the road of life, is wearied and driven in the pursuit of fame and profit, and so most easily sinks and falls.

Whenever you are with others, you should adapt your method to the occasion and use different approaches to guide and help them, so that they awaken and turn toward goodness and practice it. It is like rousing someone from a long night of nightmare; it is like rescuing him from the choking smoke and raging flame of affliction, so that body and mind are cooled and refreshed. The benefit you bring him in this way is the greatest of all.

Han Yu said: "By a word one urges people for a single age; by a book one urges them for a hundred generations." This is the way of "urging others to be good" through good words and good books. Compared with the "practicing goodness with others" spoken of earlier, it does bear the outward mark of persuasion; but because it prescribes the remedy according to the ailment, it often works wonders, and so it cannot be discarded. "Practicing goodness with others" and "urging others to be good" are the two methods of teaching by action and by word — which of the two to adopt must be judged according to the particular circumstances. If we urge a person whom words cannot move, we waste our words; if we do not urge a person whom words would move, we lose the person. Either to waste our words or to lose the person is unwise, and we ought to reflect upon this.

What does it mean to rescue people in peril? Disaster and hardship befall each of us from time to time. Once you see another amid disaster and hardship, you should feel that suffering as your own and hasten to deliver him — either by clearing away the injustice and oppression he endures, or by devising every means to free him from his plight. Mr. Cui said: "The kindness you show people need not be great; what matters is to give it quickly when they are in urgent need." Truly, these are the words of one filled with loving-kindness!

What does it mean to carry out works of great benefit? Within a single village or within a whole district, whatever is of benefit to the multitude should rightly be carried out. Either dig canals for irrigation, guide the water to ward off floods, or raise dikes against the flood; either build and repair bridges for the convenience of travelers, or offer tea and rice to relieve the hungry and thirsty. Whenever there is an opportunity, urge everyone, according to the circumstances, to join in building the work; and for your part, do not shun suspicion, do not shrink from hardship, but bear toil and resentment alike.

What does it mean to give away wealth to create blessings? In the Buddhist path, of all conduct and practice, giving is the first. What is called "giving" is, in its essence, nothing more than a single word: letting go.

The truly clear and penetrating person lets go within of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, clinging to them no longer; he lets go without of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and thought, tempted by them no longer; all that he possesses he gives up entirely. If we are not yet able to "let go of the six sense organs within, the six objects of sense without, and surrender all that we possess," then we must begin with the giving away of material goods.

All people in the world live by clothing and food, so wealth is what they value most. Yet I give away the very wealth the world prizes most: within, to break my own stinginess; without, to relieve others in peril. At first it is somewhat against the grain, but in time one becomes calm and at ease. In this way one most thoroughly washes clean the encrusted defilement of selfish desire, and most thoroughly removes the evil habits of greed and miserliness that spring from clinging to a "self."

What does it mean to safeguard the true Dharma? The true Dharma is the genuine Way. It is the eye of living beings through all generations, enabling them to see the right road of life. Without the true Dharma, how could one take part in the transforming and nurturing work of heaven and earth? How could one manage and choose among all things? How could one cast off the desires of the senses and break through affliction? How could one govern the world? And how could one awaken and rise above the mundane realm?

Therefore, whenever you see the temples, halls, paintings, and images of the sages, or the sutras and classic texts, you should hold them in reverence and repair and arrange them. As for spreading the true Dharma to repay the profound kindness of the Buddha, this above all calls for earnest exertion.

What does it mean to honor superiors and elders? Toward our fathers and elder brothers at home, toward the sovereign and officials of the state, and toward all those advanced in years, in virtue, in rank, and in insight, we should pay particular heed and serve them with reverence.

In serving one's parents at home, one should have a deeply loving heart and a gentle, agreeable countenance, speaking softly and humbly. In time this becomes second nature, and it is the very root of the harmonious spirit that moves Heaven's heart.

When governing abroad, do not imagine that the sovereign does not know, and so grow arrogant and unrestrained in whatever you do; and when interrogating a prisoner, do not imagine that the sovereign does not know, and so throw your weight about. "Serve the sovereign as you would serve Heaven" — this is a maxim of the ancients. One must be reverent and sincere, daring no trace of deceit or presumption, for it is here that hidden virtue counts for the most.

Consider the families known for loyalty and filial piety: their descendants endure for generations without break, numerous and flourishing. Therefore one must be careful and circumspect in fulfilling loyalty and filial piety to the utmost.

What does it mean to cherish living beings? At root, what makes a human being human is simply the heart of compassion — the capacity to grieve for the misfortune of others and of creatures. To seek benevolence is to seek this compassionate heart; to accumulate virtue is to accumulate this compassionate heart.

The Rites of Zhou says: "In the sacrifices of the first month, do not use female animals," for at that time they are often carrying young. Mencius says: "The noble person keeps away from the kitchen, so as not to hear the sounds of slaughter." The reason the Rites of Zhou and Mencius speak thus is precisely to preserve our heart of compassion.

For this reason our predecessors set down the "four abstentions" from eating: do not eat what you have heard being killed; do not eat what you have seen being killed; do not eat what you have raised yourself; and do not eat what was killed expressly for you. As their juniors, even if we cannot yet abstain from meat entirely, we should follow our predecessors in beginning with the four abstentions, so as to nurture our heart of compassion. As this compassionate heart gradually grows, we will come to realize that not only should killing and eating meat be refrained from, but even tiny insects must on no account be harmed, for like us human beings they breathe and live.

To obtain silk, great numbers of silkworm pupae are boiled to death; to till the fields, great numbers of insects, ants, and earthworms are killed. We should reflect that the origins of our clothing and food all lie in slaughtering these innocent lives to sustain ourselves, and therefore the sin of wantonly wasting things is equal to that of killing and eating meat. As for the lives that perish when accidentally harmed by our hands or trampled under our feet, no one can know how many they are, and we should all seek every means to avoid such harm. An old poem says: "So tender of the mice that I fear they go hungry, I often leave scraps of rice in the corner; so piteous of the moths that I fear they will fly into the flame, I light no lamp at night." How full of compassion this is!
The kinds of good deeds are endless and cannot be described one by one; but if one accomplishes these ten kinds of good deeds and then extends them further, then all virtues may be made complete.

blocks.text: Part Four — The Fruits of Humility

inline.s: The Book of Changes says: "The way of Heaven diminishes the proud and increases the humble; the way of the earth diminishes the proud and fills up the humble; the way of the spirits and gods harms the proud and blesses the humble; the way of humans dislikes the proud and loves the humble." Because humility is of such vital importance, among the sixty-four hexagrams of the Book of Changes only the hexagram Moderateness (Qian) has all six lines auspicious, whereas in the other hexagrams there are both auspicious and inauspicious lines. The Book of History, too, says: "Pride brings loss; humility receives increase."

I have gone many times with many others to take the examinations, and whenever I saw a scholar who was about to pass and rise in the world, his countenance was sure to shine with the radiance of humility.

In the xinwei year, provincial graduates from all parts gathered in the capital for the metropolitan examination for the jinshi degree. From our Jiashan county there were altogether ten candidates, and among them was one, Ding Jingyu, the youngest of them all, who was extremely humble.

Thereupon I said to Fei Jinpo: "Ding Jingyu is certain to pass this year." Fei Jinpo asked: "How do you know?" I replied: "Only the humble can receive blessings. Of these ten men, which one is like him in being honest and sincere, never daring to take precedence over anyone? Which one is like him in deferring with respect and accepting, careful and humble? Which one is like him in not replying when insulted and not arguing when slandered? If a person can be like this, even heaven and earth and the spirits and gods will protect him — how could he fail to rise?" When the list was posted, Ding Jingyu indeed passed.

In the dingchou year, in the capital, I lodged in the same place as Feng Kaizhi, and I saw that he was open-minded as a valley and dignified in bearing, having greatly changed the frivolous and arrogant faults of his youth. Li Jiyan was an upright, honest, and helpful friend who often reproved his faults to his face, and I saw that he accepted it calmly and never offered a word in his own defense. I told him: "When a person is to have good fortune, it is sure to show its signs first; when a person is to have misfortune, it is sure to show its omens. So long as the heart is humble and reverent, Heaven is sure to assist him. You will certainly pass this year." Before long he indeed passed.

Zhao Yufeng, whose given name was Guangyuan, came from Guan County in Shandong. Before he was twenty he sat the provincial examination and won the juren degree, yet for a long while he could not pass the metropolitan examination. His father was sent to serve as registrar of Jiashan County, and he followed his father to his post. There, because he greatly admired the scholarship of Mr. Qian Mingwu, he took his own essays to call on Mr. Qian. Little did he expect that Mr. Qian, taking up his brush, would blot them out as he read, until the entire essay had been struck through and not a single passage was found worthy. Zhao Yufeng was not in the least angered, but admired from the depths of his heart the quickness of Mr. Qian's intelligence, and he at once rewrote all his essays. The following year he passed the metropolitan examination.

In the renchen year, I went to the capital to have an audience with the emperor, and I met Xia Jiansuo. I saw that he was open-minded and respectful, the radiance of humility upon his face at its brightest. When I returned home I told my friends: "Whenever Heaven intends to make a person prosper, it first opens his wisdom before he receives the blessings. Once wisdom opens, even the frivolous become steady and honest, and the willful become upright and humble. Xia Jiansuo is gentle and good to such a degree that Heaven is surely going to make him prosper." When the list was posted, he indeed passed the metropolitan examination.

Zhang Weiyan of Jiangyin County was learned and extensive in his reading, wrote fine essays, and was well known among scholars. In the jiawu year he sat the provincial examination for the juren degree at Nanjing, lodging in a temple. When the list was posted and his name was not on it, in a fury he cursed the examiners for having eyes that could not see, unable to tell a good essay from a poor one.

At that time a Daoist was standing by, smiling, and Zhang turned his anger upon him. The Daoist said: "Sir, your essay is certainly not well written." Zhang, all the angrier, said: "You have not even seen my essay — how do you know it is not well written?" The Daoist said: "I have heard people say that what matters most in an essay is that the mind and breath be at peace. Now that I hear your angry cursing, I know your mind and breath are extremely ill at ease, so how could your essay possibly be well written?" The Daoist's words struck home at once, and Zhang could not help being convinced, so he stepped forward and respectfully asked for his guidance.

The Daoist said: "Whether you pass or not depends entirely on fate. If fate does not destine you to pass, then however fine your essays, they are of no use. You must make a transformation in yourself." Zhang said: "Since it is fate, how can it be transformed?" The Daoist said: "The one who builds up fate is Heaven; the one who draws its design is yourself. If you will only earnestly practice good deeds and broadly accumulate hidden virtue, what blessing is there that cannot be sought and found?"

Zhang said: "But I am a poor scholar — what am I able to do?" The Daoist said: "Good deeds and hidden merit are both created by the mind. If you can always hold fast this heart of doing good and cultivating hidden merit, then your merit will be immeasurable. Moreover, a virtue such as humility costs nothing — why do you not look into yourself, and instead go and curse the examiner?"

From then on Zhang bitterly reformed his former faults and disciplined himself in self-cultivation. Day by day his good deeds were all the more cultivated, and day by day his virtue was all the more deepened. After three more years, in the dingyou year, he dreamed that he came to a tall and spacious house, where he saw a register with many blank lines in the middle, and he asked the person beside him about it. That person answered: "This is the roll of those admitted in this year's examination." Zhang asked: "Why are so many names missing?" The person replied: "In the underworld those who take the examinations are examined once every three years. Only those who have accumulated virtue and done no evil are admitted. The names missing at the front of this book are all those who should have been admitted, but were struck off because of misconduct in recent times."

The person pointed to a line farther back and said: "In these three years you have disciplined yourself and cultivated your character with considerable care, so perhaps you should fill this vacancy. I hope you will take care of yourself." In that year's provincial examination Zhang indeed passed, as the one hundred and fifth on the list.

From this we can see that three feet above one's head there must be spirits, and that to pursue good fortune and avoid calamity is entirely within our own power. One must keep a heart of goodness, restrain one's conduct, and in the smallest degree give no offense to heaven, earth, ghosts, and spirits; and further be open-minded and humble, so that heaven, earth, ghosts, and spirits always cherish and pity one. Only then is there a foundation for receiving blessings. Those who are proud and self-satisfied surely lack broad and far-reaching charity of heart, and even if they rise in the world they gain no real enjoyment.

Therefore even a person of modest insight will not bear to narrow his own breadth of mind and so drive blessings away. Moreover, the humble and courteous can receive instruction from others, gathering in all that is good and drawing without limit on the strengths of others — and this above all is something that those engaged in study cannot do without.

blocks.text: 3. A Summary of the Whole Work

inline.s: The ancients said: "He who is resolved upon distinction will surely gain distinction; he who is resolved upon wealth and honor will surely gain wealth and honor." A person's resolve is like the root of a tree: only when the root is deep can the branches and leaves flourish and the fruit hang thick. Once this resolve is fixed, one should be humble and considerate in every thought and accommodating to others everywhere. In this way one will naturally move heaven and earth, and the creation of blessings will rest with oneself.

Now those who seek to pass the examinations have from the outset not truly fixed their resolve; it is no more than a passing fancy. When the fancy stirs they pursue it, and when the fancy fades they stop.

Mencius said to King Xuan of Qi: "If Your Majesty delights in music to the very utmost, then you will share your joy with the people; for only by sharing your joy with the people can you truly enjoy it. If you can share your joy with the people, then the whole state will be of one mind, of one virtue and one strength, and the state of Qi will soon be rich among its people and powerful in its realm!" I see that distinction in the examinations is just the same.
